title: [Quantization] Calculate Scale and Offset based on the histogram
author: rdzhabarov
body: Currently, we profile all nodes in a graph and capture both min/max as well as the histogram. Quantization scale and offset are calculated based on the global min and global max and do not take histogram into consideration. This does not work very well when there are outliers. There was the logic for calculating scale and offset based on histogram but it was removed: b5d9385 As it did not properly work. Ex, simple tensor with {1, 2} values.

title: Implement Optimal fp32-i32 Multiplication in Integer Instructions
author: hegemanjwh2
body: I have a quip doc on this issue, but here is the summary: Given a 32-bit floating-point numbers and a 32-bit integer number, we need a general-purpose method of multiplying them using only integer operations.  This is for the case where we have quantized operations running on hardware without a fast FPU or other floating-point support.  The current implementation of this only works well for particular cases of rescaling operations -- it tends to be slightly incorrect when we are performing a multiplication of a floating-point scale with an integer register in which some quantities have been accumulated, for instance as happens during a matrix multiplication (FC) or convolution operation. The overall idea here is that we want to maximize the precision we can maintain when transforming an fp32-i32 multiply into a product of two i32's.  At present, we have a general idea that we want to: (A) Select parameters for pre- and post-multiplication shifting, in order to account for scaling either up or down by factors of 2. (B) Select an appropriately-precise integer approximation to the mantissa of the f32. (C) At runtime, compute the f32-i32 product by multiplying the integer approximation to the mantissa with the i32 input, and then shifting appropriately to convert the value to the correct scale w.r.t. powers of 2. The above is the general theoretical approach.  However, in practice, we run into several technical issues. =========  The following is wrong ========= (i) Especially for right-shifting, which is the common case (because the integer approximation to the f32 mantissa is usually going to be a "scaled-up" version of the actual mantissa, in order to achieve precision), arithmetic right-shifting is not quite equivalent to [integer] division by a power of 2.  It is equivalent, as desired, for positive values; however, the truncation of right-shifting inherently rounds downward toward negative infinity, and hence is not symmetric about 0.  This is undesirable.  One solution to this is to add a certain quantity to negative i32 values prior to [arithmetic] right-shifts.  The correct value to add is 1_[input < 0] << (shift - 1), which is effectively equivalent to dividing by the respective power of 2, adding 1/2, and then truncating (when the operation is thought of as taking place over the real numbers).  This thus implements "round to nearest" behavior for negative i32 values.  (Whereas we still have "round down" behavior for postive i32 values -- however, at least... ========== END WRONG PART =========== (ii) In the course of multiplications which result from a floating-point value and an integer value which has been accumulated (possibly from other integer products), predicting the correct scale of precision on which to operate is difficult, if not impossible.  For example, suppose that we wish to multiply an f32 (whose value is known at compile-time), and an i32 (whose value is not known at compile-time) which is the result of a row-column dot product during a matrix multiply operation.  Even if the matrix entries in question are i8's, each such element-wise product can have up to 16 bits, and the dimensions of the matrix in question may also introduce another element of variance in the size of the integer that results (and which we wish to multiply by the f32).  For instance: Generally:  f = s * (i - o) For matrix multiply: f_d = \sum f_l * f_r = (s_l * s_r) * (\sum (i_l - o_l) * (i_r - o_r)) and hence i_d = (s_l * s_r / s_d) * (\sum (i_l - o_l) * (i_r - o_r)) + o_d The floating-point value in question then in s_l * s_r / s_d, which is known at compile-time.  However --  even though perhaps the number of elements in the summation may be known ahead of time -- the fact that the individual entries i_l and i_r (and consequently i_l - o_l and i_r - o_r) cannot be means that the actual order of magnitude, in bits, of the resulting i32 multiplicand can only be bounded within some range, and since we only have 32 bits to work with in the first place, it is easy to see how this could become problematic if assumptions about the actual order of the resultant i32 dot product are made at compile-time.  It therefore appears that at least some runtime analysis may be needed.

title: Thousands of libjit_stacked_kernelXXX doing the same thing are issued
author: qcolombet
body: I was looking at the llvm IR produced by the image classifier using tests/images/run.sh and I noticed that we issue thousands of this kernel: define internal void @libjit_stacked_kernel.1575(float* noalias) { entry: br label %loop loop:                                             ; preds = %loop, %entry %1 = phi i64 [ , %entry ], [ %nextvar, %loop ] %2 = call float @libjit_splat_kernel_f(i64 %1, float SomeNumber, float* null, float* null) %buffer.element.addr = getelementptr float, float* %0, i64 %1 store float %2, float* %buffer.element.addr %nextvar = add nuw nsw i64 %1, SomeOtherNumber %loopcond = icmp ult i64 %nextvar, AnotherNumber br i1 %loopcond, label %loop, label %afterloop, !llvm.loop ! afterloop:                                        ; preds = %loop ret void } Would be nice to reuse them if at all possible (haven't checked but the code seems duplicated quite a lot), so that we reduce our memory footprint and our compile time.

title: [Feature request] Tensor attributes
author: jsubag
body: It would be useful to have more attributes on tensor objects. Specifically, whether a tensor is an input/output for the function and whether its constant or mutable during inference etc. Alternatively this could be added as a utility function that backends can invoke.

title: [Feature request] Backend-specific tensors
author: jsubag
body: Backends should be able to implement their own type of tensor objects. A good example for using this feature would be having tensors backed by OpenCL resources for the OpenCL backend (and similarly for other backends). In order to support this, the Tensor class can be made more suitable for deriving (adding virtual qualifiers etc.) or create a Tensor interface class for other implementations to derive from. Additional features for this Tensor interface should include support for lock/unlock (map/unmap) or some other forms of synchronization mechanism.

title: Need to canonicalize or optimize high-dim concat to concat+transpose
author: nadavrot
body: The picture below depicts a concat node that joins nodes on dimension number 1. The IR that we generate for this code is inefficient for two reasons. First, we can't optimize the operator that writes the result because the result is scattered across the 2st dimension (dim zero is the first). And second, we emit a sequence of insert_tensor instructions that process the tensor several times invalidating cache. A much better way would be to represent this as dim-0 concat followed by a transpose. Design question:  I am not sure if this should be the canonical representation, the only representation or simply a target specific optimization.

title: Support ahead-of-time compilation of partitioned graphs
author: bertmaher
body: As discussed briefly in #1325 we need a way to perform AOT compilation of partitioned graphs.  In its simplest form (serial execution), this process looks like: for each function F:   emit code for F create main function G for each function F:   add call(F) to G  Even this fairly trivial implementation requires some refactoring to get there.  In particular, the interface to BundleSaver is too simple; it simply consumes an IRFunction and emits a .o and .weights in an output directory. We could simply punt this problem to the build tool: slurp in all the generated .os, generate C code to call each of them in turn, then compile that.  That solution seems too hacky.  The expectation should be to produce a single .o for a single network; partitioning should be transparent. Some refactoring shall be needed ;-). I don't quite know enough LLVM yet to recommend the One True Way to do this, but I suspect we'll want an LLVMIRGen (and the llvm::Module contained therein) to last through the emission of several IRFunctions.  Incrementally perform codegen and add the result to the module, recording enough information along the way to emit calls.  Finally, emit calls for the "umbrella" function, and write the module to an object file.

title: Potential problem in the quantization flow in case of broadcasting
author: tlepley-cadence
body: In Glow, the quantization is done in two passes:  profile generation quantization profile loading, and quantized model inference  Our understanding is that this mechanism works with the assumption that the IR graph at profile generation is exactly the same as the IR graph at profile loading. This is due to the fact that the quantization profile refers to node/tensor names. The assumption may not be always true because loading a model with broadcasting may result in a different graph depending on whether it is created for a batch of input data or not. In case of broadcasting with batching, there will for instance be extra Reshape/Tile nodes in the graph. In our case, we've got a runtime failure at profile load time in the following situation:  the profile was generated from one single image inferring the quantized model was done with multiple images (batching).  If generating a quantization profile with a single image is not a realistic use case, it shows anyway that there is a potential caveat here. A more realistic use case is to create the quantization profile from a batch of inputs data and to infer the quantized model with a single input data (no batch). In this case, we've got not errors at run-time because the extra tensor info in the profile was simply not used at profile loading, but it may change in with other models, or in the future if the graph optimizer performs a deeper rework of the graph in case of Reshape/Tile nodes (the optimizer is called before profile generation/load). @aturetsk

title: Glow should provide its own implementation of a random number generator to ensure deterministic testing and avoid platform-dependent differences
author: opti-mix
body: Glow currently uses the Mersenne Twister engine, which is std::mt19937. It turns out that this random number generator seeded with the same values generates different random numbers depending on the OS, e.g. it produces different results on MacOS and Linux. Most likely, the implementation of std::mt19937 is somehow platform-dependent. To avoid such problems in the future, Glow could use its own in-tree implementation of a random-number generation, which has no target dependencies. It can even be an implementation of mt19937.

title: AllocationsInfo allocates buffers for all module variables.
author: nadavrot

I think that this is okay for the JIT, but not so great for the AOT compilation because the unrelated variables become a part of the interface. For more details see: AllocationsInfo::allocateWeightVars.

title: About default compilation flags : -Wnon-virtual-dtor -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti
author: tlepley-cadence
body: We tried to compile with Glow some code that was developed outside of Glow. We've got compilation errors due to some of the default C++ compilation flags defined in glow/cmake/modules/GlowDefaults.cmake: set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} -Wall -Wnon-virtual-dtor -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti")  Is there a deep reason in Glow to disable exceptions and to have non virtual destructors ? title: Make the execution of the Glow compiler more deterministic between multiple runs
author: opti-mix
body: There are certain parts of the compiler that expose some levels of non-determinism. And I don't mean by this that numeric results of running an NN model are non-deterministic. Instead, I mean that some observable (via logs, traces, debug prints) decisions made by the compiler internally may be non-deterministic. For example, many backends statically assign memory addresses to weights and activations. The order in which these addresses are assigned depends on the order of iteration over the set of weights/activations defined by a given graph/function. And these objects are currently often hold in e.g. unordered maps. As a result, the iteration order is non-deterministic and Glow may statically assign different addresses to the same weight/activation if you'd run it multiple times on the same inputs. This kind of non-determinism is very annoying, because it complicates the debugging and makes comparing the traces produced by different runs of the compiler (e.g. by means of -debug-glow-only=xyz) very difficult. The aim of this issue is therefore:  Identify the places where we have this kind of non-determinism Fix such issues by e.g. using data structures with a deterministic iteration order (map instead of unordered_map, etc). Depending on the case, we may want to either use such a deterministic data structure either for the whole duration of the compilation or only inside the code snippet that exposes the non-deterministic behavior.

title: [Glow Runtime] Top Level Task
author: qcolombet
body: This is the top level issue to track all the work we plan to do to make the glow runtime supports concurrent execution, pipelining, batching and so on. At a high level, the idea for the runtime is to be able to:  Enqueue inputs: Run input0, then run input1 as soon as the previous run is done, etc. Slice the inputs into batch size and transparently run them: Take N input and sequentially run them in batches of M (where M is the size of the compiled model and N the actual run size.) Pipeline work across models: Run input1 on model M1, then run the result of M1 on M2 while running input2 on M1, etc.  Among other things, the glow runtime will have to:  Manage input/output queues for each model (and communication with the devices) Manage incoming model Keep track of data dependencies and schedule next tasks to be done Split inputs Pad inputs Dispatch workload on device Keep track of the status of devices Also, somewhat orthogonal to the runtime, but related, glow will need to: Determine what and where to run things (graph partitioning)  Right now, we started by splitting the compilation and runtime stages properly. This work is tracked in: #2040, #1967, #1953, #1951

title: [RFC] Specialized precision specification
author: jfix71
body: Some models may need a specialized precision specification. For example, right now we have very coarse grained options to quantize all of a model/convert all of a model to fp16 (modulo node kinds specified as "keep original precision"). However, some models may require nodes of the same kind to have different precision (e.g. some Add nodes should use fp16, others int8). It seems the best way to specify this is to allow for a user to provide a precision specification file that designates what precision each node in the graph should have. Each node's name (from the proto they are loaded from) would be specified along with the node's desired precision. Some initial questions/brainstorming here:   When should this specification file be loaded and applied? Because some operators are implemented as many nodes, it seems we will need to do this as we build the graph. Thus there is likely a data structure (e.g. a map from nodes to output types) that will need to be passed from node builder to a FunctionConverter.   Related to 1, an operator may be implemented as multiple Glow nodes internally by the graph creator (e.g. createBatchedReduceMean() creates a BatchedReduceAdd, Splat, and Div, and only the Div is returned). Do we apply the same precision to all nodes created?   Assuming yes to 2, creating the aforementioned map from nodes to types is not straightforward using our current API and nodes, because if an operator is implemented via multiple nodes then only the final node in the chain is returned by the creator. Some initial thoughts on solutions:  Change the node creator API to return a structure that holds all the nodes created by a call. At first thought this is a bit problematic, as it could potentially greatly complicate the importers and unit tests. Change the node creator API to pass in an optional empty set ptr, which has all newly created nodes added to it. This seems kind of meh to me, but also perhaps the least intrusive and wouldn't require extra walking of the graph like iii, and no extra overhead of new nodes in the graph like iv. Save a running set of the nodes in the graph prior to calling the creator and then compare against the new graph to determine the new nodes to add to the mapping. I don't really love this option, but it at least requires no API change to the node creators. Stop implementing operators directly as many different nodes in the creator and instead add actual nodes for them, which are later lowered. The lowered nodes would use the same precision as their parent node. This means we'd need to consider/handle more nodes across the compiler infrastructure, e.g. we'd likely need to extend graph optimizations to consider them, etc.    Should we require the quantization parameters to be declared in this precision specification? This means there is manual intervention required if we want to get the quantization parameters via our own profiling. Alternatively, we could specify the integer width (e.g. int8), and then require a quantization profile file to be loaded as well for any nodes that should be quantized. I suppose we could support both.

title: Can we stop lowering FC to Matmul+BatchedAdd?
author: bertmaher
body: GEMM is almost always implemented as Y = AX+b, so we actually end up doing something less efficient by separating these into two nodes.  It's pretty universal on HW backends, too.  We could write new optimizations to re-fuse them, but why?

title: Delay the 'Quantize(Constant)->Constant' optim until after post-lowering.
author: tlepley-cadence
body: Currently, Constant are statically quantized early in the compilation flow. Basically the Quantize(Constant)->Constant optim happens in the glow::optimize() function. There are multiple issues with this, potentially resulting into accuracy loss because the scale/offset of Constant may still have to change during the Glow compilation flow. By keeping Quantize nodes longer in the IR, scale/offset can be changed freely without resulting into any accuracy loss for constants. In particular, the backend may at post-lowering:  introduce rescale nodes to handle specific constrains between node operands for the target, resulting to the need to requantize some constants after rescale propagation / optims. do extra target specific optimizations resulting in the need to requantize some constants.  Just to illustrate with an example, the convolution bias is currently quantized to have a scale equal to (scale of input) * (scale of weights). We noticed that after post-lowering this equality was not necessary true anymore, due to some lowering & optimization combinations. the bias then needs to be requantized, what can be done without loss only if the Quantize node is still in the IR. See: #2166 @beicy

title: [ONNXIFI][GraphAPI] Add "orErr" methods for graph creation api
author: jackm321
body: Add additional graph creation methods that will return a llvm::Expected<Node *> and return an error instead of asserting if a precondition is not met. These new methods should be called by the model loading layer only. Ideally any errors that arise during loading should be caught by check within the loaders themselves and these new graph creation methods are intended as a last line of defense before to catch any malformed inputs before they are transformed into the glow high level IR, beyond which all nodes should be considered valid.

title: [ONNXIFI] Add additional precondition checks to model loaders
author: jackm321
body: Model loaders should verify preconditions for the nodes they are loading (ONNX or Caffe2) before invoking the glow graph creation api methods. To make a concrete example, ONNXModelLoader::loadConv() should check the dimensions of the filterValue to ensure that they are valid instead of relying on the graph creation API's assertConvDims called from Function::createConv() to find errors.

title: [ONNXIFI] Handle out of memory errors in onnxInitGraph
author: jackm321
body: Create an out of memory error and return this error from HostManager::addNetwork in the event that enough memory could not be allocated to initialize the network. This error should be handled by glow's ONNXIFI interface and a ONNXIFI_STATUS_NO_SYSTEM_MEMORY status should be returned.

title: Eliminate LiveIntervalsInstructionNumbering
author: stoklund
body: Now that Glow's linear IR is implemented with a TaggedList, it is no longer necessary to maintain the auxiliary instruction numbering maps in the LiveIntervalsInstructionNumbering class — two instruction iterators can be compared directly to determine which instruction comes first in the function. The LiveIntervalsInstructionNumbering class also makes it possible to distinguish between READ_SLOT and WRITE_SLOT positions. It is not completely obvious that this is needed; LLVM only needs the slots to deal with exotic early clobber constraints on inline assembly, and Cranelift doesn't need slots. If necessary, the slots can be represented with a PointerIntPair consisting of an instruction pointer and the slot number. The begin/end members of the Interval class can be replaced with instruction pointers (or the PointerIntPair if necessary).

title: Graph Partitioning
author: beicy

title: Use static registry pattern for backends/device managers
author: bertmaher
body: Right now we have to explicitly add all supported backends to switch tables in createBackend (and createDeviceManager).  It'd be nice to use a static registry pattern (I think https://www.bfilipek.com/2018/02/factory-selfregister.html is a decent overview of this pattern) to allow backends to register their existence at startup.  That will also break an annoying dependence cycle where Backend depends on DeviceSpecificBackend and vice versa, because the interface and factory dependences go either direction. It'd also be worthwhile to look at how LLVM solves this problem with its backends, since LLVM usually does things The Right Way.

title: ExecutionEngine::compile() modifies Function
author: geoffberry
body: If a backend implements transformPreLowering() or transformPostLowering(), the Function parameter to ExecutionEngine::compile() is modified in place, so subsequent calls to ExecutionEngine::compile() with the same function will get the transformed Function as input.  This can lead to problems if the function is compiled with different backends or if the backend transforms aren't prepared to handle the backend-specific nodes they may produce as input.

title: Implementing quantization ops for server side models.
author: beicy

title: More general implementation of Row/ChannelWiseWQuantization
author: ayermolo
body: I would like to propose a generic approach for ‘RowWise’ quantization, that gives in addition the possibility for the backend to perform some customizations. I’ve created a WIP PR with a prototype implementation for review/discussion #2480. Currently a specific ‘RowWise’ node type variant has been created for each operation concerned by rowwise quantization: RowwiseQuantizedFullyConnected/RowwiseQuantizedSparseLengthsWeightedSum. Going by this approach if we want to apply it to regular Convolution we would create ChannelWiseQuantizedConvolution, or something like that. Our proposal is to add a generic ChannelWiseQuantization node instead of creating a specific node variant each time we want to support rowwise quantization. The input of ChannelWiseQuantization would be quantized weights, original floating point weight,  scales array, and offsets array. The latter two can either be in tensor or internal vector type to the node. We keep the original floating point weight tensor since some backend may want to do a custom quantization. Keeping original weights around can be removed down the road if we change infrastracture of glow to allow backends hooks to quantize on node level. I included Interpreter and CPU backend implementations for illustrative purposes. During LLVM generation it would allow:  backends to use this information to select appropriate function for the target device, and pass relevant information in to it. various optimizations to deal with only one node type, vs bunch of different node types of RowwiseQuantized variety

title: [RFC] Support for multiple training algorithms
author: SplitInfinity
body: Preface In #2524, I added support for the Adagrad training algorithm in preparation for adding training support for SparseLengthsWeightedSum in #2541. The design I chose was not well-received, so I want to propose a new design based on the feedback in that PR and discuss it before I update the PR. Problem Statement glow::differentiate adds SGDNodes for every trainable Placeholder in a Graph that calculate the new updated values based on the stochastic gradient descent algorithm. It also adds SaveNodes to save these updated values back into their corresponding Placeholders. However, this approach does not allow Glow to support multiple training algorithms (i.e. multiple ways to compute new weights). Proposal There is a simple POD struct named TrainingConfig that includes a bunch of parameters used by stochastic gradient descent: struct TrainingConfig {   float L1Decay{0};   float L2Decay{0};   float learningRate{0.01f};   float momentum{0.0};   unsigned batchSize{1}; };  This struct is passed into glow::differentiate and used to construct SGDNodes with the proper learning rate, momentum, etc. I propose that we replace this with the following: class Trainer { public:   Trainer(float learningRate, unsigned batchSize) : learningRate_(learningRate), batchSize_(batchSize) {}   virtual bool instrument(Function* F, PlaceholderBindings& bindings) = 0; protected:   // Parameters used by multiple subclasses   float learningRate_{0.01f};   unsigned batchSize_{1}; };  New training algorithms are implemented as follows: // Stochastic gradient descent class SGDTrainer : final Trainer { public:   SGDTrainer(float learningRate, unsigned batchSize, float L1Decay, float L2Decay, float momentum) : Trainer(learningRate, batchSize), L1Decay_(L1Decay), L2Decay_(L2Decay), momentum_(momentum) {}   bool instrument(Function* F, PlaceholderBindings& bindings) override {     // code here to add SGDNode to F, save new weights into Placeholders, etc.     // return true if instrumentation was successful   } private:   float L1Decay{0};   float L2Decay{0};   float momentum{0.0}; };  // Adagrad class AdagradTrainer : final Trainer { public:   AdagradTrainer(float learningRate, unsigned batchSize, float epsilon) : Trainer(learningRate, batchSize), epsilon_(epsilon) {}   bool instrument(Function* F, PlaceholderBindings& bindings) override {     // code here to add Adagrad to F, create new Placeholders to store momentum history, etc.     // return true if instrumentation was successful   } private:   float epsilon_{1e-5}; };  glow::differentiate would accept a reference/pointer to Trainer and use it as follows: // Clone the function to produce the training version of it. auto *G = F->clone(newFunctionName); ... // Insert grad nodes. ... // Add training instrumentation. bool ok = trainer->instrument(G, bindings);  if (!ok) {   // report error, assert, etc. }  Open Questions  Should there be getters/setters for the algorithm parameters of Trainer and its subclasses? There is some code that currently reads them out of a TrainingConfig object, but that's easy enough to modify so that there are other variable in the same scope as TrainingConfig that store those values.

title: OpenCL backend should use different GPU memory buffers for constant weights and for any run specific data
author: opti-mix
body: OpenCL backend currently statically allocates before the first run one big GPU buffer to hold all the constant weights, mutable weights and activations. This approach is not the best idea if this backend should ever be used for processing  multiple requests for the same NN model, because each run needs its own buffer for mutable weights and allocations, but could reuse the constant weights. Thus, the backend should allocate separate buffers for the constant weights and for the run-specific data. Specifically, something like this needs to be done:   Each kernel named ...W (i.e. a kernel invoked directly from the OpenCL.cpp) gets as many __global void * parameters as we have different GPU buffers for a run (e.g. __global void *constantMem, __global void *mutableMem). These pointers will be used as base pointers into corresponding memory regions   Buffer operands of these kernels should now indicate which memory buffer they belong to (e.g. they should indicate if they are constant or mutable). The simplest possible solution could be to pass a flag per such operand to indicate this information, but this could be rather annoying.  The buffer operands are currently passed as offsets into the buffers they belong to. One could "misuse" the highest bits of these values to encode the type of the buffer (constant, mutable, etc). It is essentially the well-known pointer tagging approach. One would use introduce e.g.CONST_ARG(arg) and MUTABLE_ARG(arg) for adding these tags to the arguments and GET_ARG_ADDRESS(const_buffer_base_address, mutable_buffer_base_address, arg) for computing the address of a buffer inside kernels    The invocations of all the updated kernels should be adjusted accordingly   The execute method that kicks off a run of the model (or more likely the OpenCL DeviceManager) should take care of allocating a single buffer for holding the constant weights and allocating a separate buffer for mutable data on a per run basis.   NOTE: Many other backends are likely to follow this approach. Share the constant data between runs to save memory and allocate separate buffers for mutable data on a per-run basis. If allocating separate buffers for mutable data on a per-run basis becomes a significant overhead (e.g. due to the increased amount of alloc/dealloc operations), one could think of using a pooling approach for these buffers.

title: Change the default format how FC (and MatMul) stores weights?
author: opti-mix
body: When we load FC from C2 models, we automatically transpose the weights, so that we have A: M x K and W:K x N And we use those layouts in the interpreter and in the CPU backend. But almost all of our HW backends (e.g. OpenCL, etc) require that W is provided in pre-transposed, so that the inputs are A:M x K and B:N x K, because this results in a much more efficient memory access pattern. To achieve that, all those HW backends  introduce their custom versions of FC, where the only difference is the transposed W. It also seems that this pre-transposed W layout may be more efficient even on CPUs, because of a more efficient memory access pattern, but this is not clear. Given all this, should we change the default for the Glow's FC node and use pre-transposed Ws? This would allow us to get rid of re-defining HW-backend specific FC nodes and may even make our CPU FCs faster. Opinions? Remark: Besides transposing W, HW may also require a HW-specific padding and alignment of each row of W. That cannot be naturally expressed using Glow's Tensors yet.

title: Teach Glow how to support custom alginment requirements for tensor dimensions
author: opti-mix
body: Some backends may have specific requirements on the alignment of data inside tensors. E.g. each row of the innermost dimension to be cache line size aligned. In principle, any of the dimensions may have an alignment requirement. Glow's Tensor class as of today is not able to represent this requirements, because they underlying Type cannot express it. Type only stores the actual dimensions, but not the aligned dimensions. So, how could one use Glow Tensors to enforce any requirements on alignments? Here are some possible alternatives:   Glow Tensors could be extended to explicitly support custom strides. Type would have a dedicated strides_ member in addition to sizes_.  This change could be useful for different backends. Any code that accesses tensor elements only via logical indices and never through raw pointers should continue to work correctly. But it may require a lot of changes all over the place, especially in libjit and some kernels and operations that iterate over the content of a tensor using raw pointers.  Everything that uses row pointers would start iterating over "padding" elements. These elementds may contain junk data and thus all such places should be updated to skip such elements. libjit kernels should get additional parameters for strides, so that they can correctly compute linear indices into tensors.      It is also possible to try tweaking the representation of tensors only in the specific backends that need it, without changing the Tensor and Type classes. E.g. one could introduce custom backend-specific Tensor classes. This is certainly doable, but it is very likely that this logic will be re-implemented in a number of different backends.    The disadvantages of this approach are:  it may require more memory to keep both the original and backend specific tensors. it may involve a lot of copying between padded and non-padded tensors none of the existing kernels can be re-used, because they work only with Glow's standard tensors.     It is also possible to use just the usual Tensor and Type classes. Every time when a custom-aligned tensor is needed, one would represent it e.g. as a Tensor with bigger dimensions that accommodate for the required alignments and contains some junk padding elements. Such a tensor would have a desired memory layout. But it is important to note that some of the existing operations on tensors would not produce correct results when applied to this tensor, because all those operations assume that all elements contain real data and need to be processed, which is not the case due to the added junk padding elements. The content of the original tensor would be copied into the "padded" tensor before the operation that makes use of custom alignments and would be copied back into the original tensor after that operation.  The disadvantages of this approach are:  it may require more memory to keep both the original and the padded tensor. it may involve a lot of copying between padded and non-padded tensors Some of the existing kernels/operations cannot be re-used with the "padded" tensors, because they would try to process "padding" elements. One would need to develop new kernels for "padded kernels"      I'm probably missing some further alternatives here. It would be interesting to hear from those who faced a similar issue what was their experience and how they solved this problem. May be we can learn from it. Personally, I tend to think that (1) is the cleanest solution, but I'm afraid it may involve a lot of re-factoring in existing kernels. Note: This issue is related to #1214.

title: Support for a heteogeneous partitioning
author: opti-mix
body: Glow's runtime currently supports partitioning of a graph between multiple devices of the same kind, i.e. controlled by the same kind of a backend. But it could be very useful to support heterogeneous partitioning as well, so that a graph could be partitioned among devices of different kinds. One specific use-case which would benefit from it is when you bring up new backends. Initially they do not support all of the ML operations. Thus, one could just partition the graph in such a way that all operations not supported by the new backend yet would be in a separate partition(s) executed by e.g. an existing, established backend (e.g Interpreter or CPU). All the operations supported by the new backend already would be in partitions executed by this backend. Done this way, it becomes very easy to perform an end-2-end testing of the whole models with a new backend even though not all operations are supported yet. One can improve this support gradually, which makes the development of a new backend more manageable.

title: [ONNXIFI] Communicate async failures across onnxifi interface
author: jackm321
body: If any failure happens while running a request asynchronously, there is no way to communicate this from Glow to C2. onnxSetIOAndRunGraph will return an error status if an error occurs before the async run request if initiated but after this there is no mechanism for errors to be reported. To fix this, onnx Events should be improved by adding two things  A status that can be set when signalling the event and retrieved in onnxGetEventState. An additional onnxWaitEventFor method that waits for some number of ms before unblocking even if the event hasn't been signalled yet so that if a request fails and doesn't signal the output event, C2 won't be blocked indefinitely.

title: isInput and isOutput checks in BackendUtils.cpp may be not very precise
author: opti-mix
body: While debugging some issues with a custom backend I discovered that isInput and isOutput report many placeholders as both inputs and outputs, at least when we talk about IRFunctions that are results of partitioning done by the Partitioner. The reason for this strange behavior seems to be related to the way how these checks are performed. It seems like currently they check if a placeholder is written to anywhere in the whole module. With this logic, it is possible that even if a given placeholder is not really used by any instruction in the IRFunction, it is still reported as input or output if it is used in any other functions. To make the checks more precise, we could do something like this: /// If \p PH is an output placeholder in the function \p F, \returns true. /// This is determined by checking if the PH has a user which uses the PH as an /// overwritten input. bool isOutput(const Placeholder *PH, const IRFunction &F) {   auto *weight = F.getWeightForNode(PH);   assert(weight && "Weight for a node was not found");   for (const auto &use : weight->getUsers()) {     OperandKind kind = use.getOperand().second;     if (kind != OperandKind::In) {       return true;     }   }   return false; }  /// If \p PH is an input placeholder in the function \p F, \returns true. bool isInput(const Placeholder *PH, const IRFunction &F) {   // Check that the PH is always used as an @in parameter by the current   // function.   auto *weight = F.getWeightForNode(PH);   assert(weight && "Weight for a node was not found");   for (const auto &use : weight->getUsers()) {     OperandKind kind = use.getOperand().second;     if (kind != OperandKind::In) {       return false;     }   }   return true; }

title: Make all useful data structures in Glow easy to dump in a textual form
author: opti-mix
body: Being able to dump any interesting data structures is very useful for interactive debugging and print debugging. Currently, many of interesting data structures (e.g. glow::Value) have dump methods. Some others, e.g. glow::Node have getDebugDesc() method, but no dump method. And many interesting data structures don't have any method to dump their content, e.g. glow::Type. Ideally, it would be nice to have the same uniform way to dump any data structure. LLVM usually uses dump for it. It is also very useful to be able to get a string representation of the dumped content of any data structure as it allows for including it into a bigger composite output consisting of many different parts. So, in short it would be nice to have e.g. the following methods for all interesting data structures in Glow:  dump(llvm::raw_ostream &os) dump() which just calls dump(llvm::raw_ostream &os) with a default output stream as a parameter std::string toString(), which dumps into string

title: [runtime] get clean on typing in the runtime
author: nickgg
body: We need to realign our interfaces in the runtime, it's a bit of a jumble right now. For example, looking at the Module provided to HostManager::addNetwork:  Its passed in as a unique_ptr provided into the provisioner as a reference (non const) The provisioner then gives it as a const raw pointer to the DeviceManager We convert it to a shared_ptr and store it in the HostManager's NetworkData During a run we store it as raw ptr in the ThreadPoolExecutor's ExecutionState.  This is basically every possible way of storing or referring to an object (I didn't see us move it onto the stack, at least). We need to go through the Runtime interfaces again and make sure we're consistent. (for the record I think we should change all the above to shared_ptr, or if we can't handle that, just use raw ptr and cross our fingers).

title: Metadata location de-duplication
author: gcatron
body: In a conversation with @opti-mix  regarding #2871 we discussed metadata. We keep the Module around in the Runtime as a metadata container. Currently this means type data, PHs and Constants. This means there is a duplication of information between the Module and RuntimeBundle. It would probably be a good idea to take a closer look at what we need at runtime and decide on one place to keep our needed metadata.

title: Implement kernel stacking for OpenCL backend
author: opti-mix
body: Launching a lot of small kernels is pretty expensive on GPUs. Therefore fusing multiple kernels together (e.g. fusing simple elementwise kenels) can result in a significantly faster execution as less kernels need to be launched.

title: AOT support for OpenCL backend
author: opti-mix
body: Currently, Glow's OpenCL backend "interprets" Glow low-level IR instructions and issues calls of different kernels. In principle, one could go over the list of IR instructions and generate a main dispatching OpenCL function for the NN model. This generated function which would perform all those kernel launches later at run-time. And this generated function is self-contained and does not need Glow to run. It only needs OpenCL shared libraries and some kernels to run. And it can be linked with/invoke from any custom application.

title: Port RecommendationSystemTest to use the HostManager
author: nickgg
body: The RecommendationSystemTest has a mode where it partitions the network and compares it to the unpartitioned results, but uses a hacky "executor" to do it. We should use the full runtime to run this test, but we can't currently configure it to partition in the right manner (no way to configure device sizes). Remove the blocker and port the partitioned tests to use the HostManager.

title: resnet-* example code should reuse Tensor memory for images
author: nickgg
body: In #2896 a version of readPngImage was added that loads into an existing Tensor. Convert the resnet example code (resnet-verify and resnet-runtime) to use this format to limit the total number of Tensors it allocates to some fixed (configurable) number. The more complex part here is how you rate limit the example code to wait until a Tensor is available.

title: [runtime] add device memory size configuration to the DeviceConfig::parameters map on all backends
author: nickgg
body: Since #2874 we have a mechanism for passing through specific options to DeviceManagers through the HostManager. One obvious configuration we may want across all devices is the ability to set the amount of available memory (useful for configuring partitioning). Add support for Device size in the DeviceConfig which configures device size in all existing DeviceManagers (Interpreter, CPU, OpenCL & Habana).

title: Provide docker container with all required dependencies installed
author: rdzhabarov
body: Providing docker container would enable fast experimentation and ramping up on Glow stack. It should include:  llvm and other dependencies installed Model/weight definition for Glow examples

author: vuzelac-cadence
body: Curios how Glow supports Pytorch models - I've filed a question to pytorch: pytorch/pytorch#20453 But also, maybe there is something to learn here, as I don't see any of examples models work when converted to ONNX.

title: How to check if a op is supported by a Backend before lowering this op
author: beicy
body: For Heterogeneous partitioning, we need to assign a op with a BackendKind before the op is lowered. Current "isOpSupported" function checks the op after lowering. Now the way is we first check if a op can be lowered and then check "isOpSuppored" . However, according to @jfix71, it is not correct: ``` "Seeing this in action, I don't think it makes sense actually. Backends will return true for Nodes they do not know about. E.g. if a backend does not support SparseLengthsWeightedSum, it will return false for isOpSupported(), but true for shouldLower() even though SparseLengthsWeightedSum isn't lowered to anything. One alternative here could be that when we encounter an unsupported node, clone it, and then try to lower it. If it's not lowered then it's unsupported. Else if it is lowered then recursively do the same check on all of the nodes added during lowering. This is going to require a non-trivial refactoring though, in lowering logic/figuring out how best to clone the Node temporarily and tracking the nodes created from lowering." We need to improve this check.  #2687

title: Support tracing in ExecutionEngine
author: jackm321
body: It would be helpful debugging performance issues with backends if the ExeuctionEngine would support tracing so that one doesn't have to manually create a HostManager. Maybe if ExecutionEngine and HostManager are eventually merged this will be a non-issue but it would be great to have support for this.

title: Memoize Type::getSliceSize
author: SplitInfinity
body: Type::getSliceSize will redo work if called repeatedly with different values for startDim. Should we memoize this function to only do work if necessary (i.e. the slice size has not been computed before in the process of computing other slice sizes?).

title: Need support for Deconvolution (Transposed convolution, ONNX ConvTranspose) node
author: vuzelac-cadence
body: Want to discuss the approach for supporting Deconvolution, needed for upsampling in some segmentation networks. I plan to add support for ONNX ConvTranspose  which nicely maps onto our backend Deconvolution. But not sure what that node should map to  in CPU/Interpreter One approach is to reuse ConvolutionGrad node (and it's libjit implementation) and just skip unrelated things (like bias gradient) by adding a flags. However, I am not sure about the performance of this implementation - Convolution is supported in various libraries and leaving this one with only the default implementation seems slow. Alternatively, input can be prepared to perform regular convolution (slicing and scattering of input, transposing weights and what not), which again is not optimal just like the above. We don't care much about any efficient implementation in CPU/Interpreter (except for the simulation speed during development) but wanted to hear if you have any plans here.

title: Add support for Argmax output of MaxPool node
author: Max-K-cadence
body: Glow does not currently support the Argmax (2nd) output of MaxPool node. The check that reports error for this case was added by pull request #1775. Is there a plan to actually support this output? There are models where it is used.

title: Problems accessing global variables in the host-process from the JITted code
author: opti-mix
body: Let's say there is a global int variable global_counter defined somewhere in the host-process using Glow JIT. And something inside the libjit needs to access this variable. The most natural way to do it would be to declare this variable as an external variable. To avoid any issues with the C++ name mangling, one would probably declare and use it like this: extern "C" int global_counter; void libjit_use_global_counter() {    global_counter++; } And then define this variable in the host-process e.g. like this: extern "C" int global_counter = 0; But if you try to build and run something like this using the -cpu backend you will discover that the address of global_counter cannot be found and thus you cannot run the JITted code.

title: Bundles should be produceable as shared objects
body: Currently, there is no way to emit bundles as shared libraries without specifying external llvm compiler. This is inconvenient. Perhaps we could use an additional option, say -shared, along with -emit-bundle to indicate that we are asking for a shared object. It seems this is possible by using -llvm-compiler to set external compiler together with the llvm-compiler-opt=-shared to add the required external compiler option. However, simply using -llvm-compiler-opt without -llvm-compiler has no effect. From BundleSaver.cpp, in BundleSaver::produceBundle():    if (!llvmCompiler.empty()) {       // Compile bitcode using an external LLVM compiler.       std::string cmd = llvmCompiler;       for (auto option : llvmCompilerOptions) {         cmd += " " + option + " ";       }       cmd += " " + bundleCodeOutput;       std::string bundleObjectCodeOutputOpt =           " -o " + (outputDir + "/" + bundleName + ".o").str();       cmd += bundleObjectCodeOutputOpt;       if (system(cmd.c_str())) {         llvm::errs() << "Error running external LLVM compiler:\n"                      << cmd << "\n";         GLOW_UNREACHABLE("Error running external LLVM compiler");       }     }  So it looks like -llvm-compiler-opt only has an effect when -llvm-compiler is specified. This makes sense, of course, but is a bit inconvenient. Again, a simple option, like -shared, along with -emit-bundle, would be better.

title: Unify RuntimeBundle and AllocationsInfo
author: opti-mix
body: The fact that there is AllocationsInfo which performs its own allocation is a recipe for disaster. We planned to switch completely to RuntimeBundle and centralize the allocation logic there. But Glow's CPU backend currently invokes allocateJITMemory and runtime::RuntimeBundle::create from LLVMBackend::compileIRWithoutConstants! This seems very odd. CPU backend should be switched completely to RuntimeBundle or AllocationsInfo should be at least implemented on top of RuntimeBundle or something like that. But there should be only once place performing the static memory allocation. cc @gcatron

title: Support for optional inputs/operands in nodes/instructions?
author: opti-mix
body: Glow generally tries to limit the amount of mandatory nodes that need to be supported by each backend. This allows for faster bootstrapping of new backends. And it limits the complexity. There are some nodes which can be expressed in terms of other nodes, but most backends would like to use a different form of them:  For example, there is FullyConnectedNode and  MatMulNode. The difference is that MatMuNodel does not have a bias parameter. Typically, Glow would lower FullyConnectedNode into MatMulNode followed by a BatchedAddNode. Another example would be the SparseLengthsWeightedSum node. SparseLengthsSum operation would be always lowered by the loader into SparseLengthsWeightedSum where the weights are all 1.0. This way Glow doesn't need to define a dedicated SparseLengthsSum node. (in reality there are 3 different SparseLengthsWeightedSum-based operations and thus Glow saves on definitions of 3 non-weighted variants of these operations). But some backends actually want to be able to use a non-weighted version SparseLengthsSum kernels because they are more efficient.  To do that, the backends may need to define backend-specific nodes or instructions to represent those non-weighted versions of the operation and eventually introduce custom graph transforms or IRGen changes (see e.g. #3039 for a discussion about this topic).  One of the problems with these examples is the fact that essentially one of the inputs/operands (e.g. bias in FC or weights in SLWS) is optional in the alternative versions of these operations. E.g. FC without a bias becomes MatMul. And SparseLengthsWeightedSum without weights becomes SparseLengthsSum. But it is currently impossible to express an optional input/operand and thus a new node or instruction is defined today. What if Glow would allow for a definition of optional inputs/operands? This idea was mentioned today in discussions with @bertmaher and @artemrakhov about these topics, so I decided to capture it in this issue. With optional inputs/operands, the number of nodes/instructions definitions does not need to be increased in many cases, but some special handling of these optional inputs/operands needs to be introduced. Specifically, the major changes would be something like this:   We could imagine that NodeGen/InstrGen could mark such operands in a special way to indicate that they can be optional and then the auto-generated code for nodes and instructions would have assertions to check of all the mandatory inputs/operands are provided, but would relax those checks for optional inputs/operands.   Of course, all the places working with such inputs/operands would need to be inspected/updated to be prepared to work with a missing input/operand. We have some examples of similar places already, e.g. those ones working with Concat nodes and the like, who have essentially a variadic number of operands.

title: Idea: rework Tile to reduce memory allocation overhead in ONNX
author: Max-K-cadence
body: Just an idea on what can be improved. Currently, Glow's Tile node currently duplicates data along 1 dimension (and corresponds to such Caffe2 operator). ONNX's tile has a vector of values that show how many times we should multiply along every dimension. It is implemented by building a chain of Tile nodes that multiply data over and over again along each dimension. Whenever we create another node, we should create its output tensor, and this is where we use redundant memory. We could rework Glow Tile node to have a vector of constants (with multiplication coefficients along each axis) to meet ONNX specification. With that, Caffe2 Tile is just a particular case of this operation with multiplication vector (1, 1, X, 1, 1). We save memory on creation of intermediate input/output tensors in ONNX Tile by doing so. As a side effect, it enables the following optimization: Y = Tile(X, (a, b, c)) Z = Tile(Y, (x, y, z))  into Z = Tile(X, (a * x, b * y, c * z))  which, I believe, is not done now.

title: Compile should take a Module, not a Function
author: jfix71
body: Currently, we have the concept of compiling a Function using the EE. This does not align with e.g. the HostManager, wherein we compile a Module instead of a Function. Additionally, when compiling a Function we do optimizations such as DCE on Constants. This is not always safe, as other Functions may still be being built (see #3141) and so Constants shouldn't be deleted so early on. In general we should compile Modules instead of Functions. We should also move optimizations like DCE for Constants out of optimizeFunction() and into a new optimizeModule() that's performed after all Functions in a Module are optimized. body: loadConcat produces a node that is not of type Constant (it is rather of type Concat which is a subclass of Storage). On the other hand, loadConstantOfShape expects a Constant node as input. So Concat followed by ConstantOfShape produces an error such as the following: ../../../lib/Importer/ProtobufLoader.cpp:79 message: could not find constant with name 43  The relevant part from an ONNX graph is:   %40 : Tensor = onnx::Unsqueeze[axes=[0]](%38)   %41 : Tensor = onnx::Unsqueeze[axes=[0]](%37)   %42 : Tensor = onnx::Unsqueeze[axes=[0]](%39)   %43 : Tensor = onnx::Concat[axis=0](%40, %41, %42)   %44 : Float(1, 1, 128) = onnx::ConstantOfShape[value={0}](%43)  Here is the snippet from loadConstantOfShape:   if (op.input_size() > 0) {     Constant *in;     ASSIGN_VALUE_OR_RETURN_ERR(in, getConstantByName(op.input(0)));  It is the last line, namely ProtobufLoader::getConstantByName that is issuing the error. title: [Optimization] Splitting FC weights to facilitate distribution of compute across multiple computational units
author: rdzhabarov
body: Problem: Given an FC operator with the input of [M;K], weights of [K;N] and bias of [N] dimensions. For certain ASIC architectures it's beneficial to split weights into several chunks and distribute it over multiple processing units. This way we could fit weights into SRAM, take advantage of parallel execution and reduce overall latency. Proposed changes: Let's consider the scenario when weights are split into two chunks: [K;N/2], [K;N/2] and distributed over two computational units during the compilation time (with the help of partitioner). Bias with the [N/2] sub tensors correspondingly. In this case:  input activations of size [M;K] needs to be copied to those two processing units during the execution. Perform 2 FCs, input [M;K], weights [K;N/2], bias [N/2] Concat results of [M;N/2] into the final tensor of size [M;N]  From Glow perspective this could be expressed as a general graph level optimizations (followed by partitioner) which can be enabled/disabled by backends if needed. Optimization needs to have a parameter specifying number of chunks to split weights and bias (mostly driven by number of computation units). As well as size of N starting from which the optimization needs to be performed. Both parameters are architecture dependent and might need to be tuned, for now we could make those as a constant and later figure out the way to set it on per backend basis. Original idea is coming from @nrsatish, please, add any details/comments if any. cc: @bertmaher @arunm-git @beicy

title: [Optimization] Operator broadcasting for element-wise operators
author: mciprian13
body: Currently when a model has element-wise operations (add,sub,mult,div,etc) between a tensor and a constant scalar, the scalar is broadcasted at import-time to match the tensor size, potentially resulting in large tensor sizes (and hence memory footprint) like in this example (the constants originate from scalars):  Furthermore, when multiple such operations are used, the graph optimizer will use run-time broadcasting like this:  The solution would be to have "smarter" implementations of the operators right at the very end (instructions) by dispatching the appropriate operator depending on the broadcasting case. For example, for a scalar x tensor multiplication, a specialized operator should be dispatched which does: mult[idx] = tensor[idx] * scalar without actually broadcasting the scalar at import/compile/run-time. This should have benefits both in terms of performance and memory footprint.
