title: Support non-square padding for Convolution operator
author: artemrakhov-glow
body: Convolution is the most important operator for Computer Vision NNs. The simplest implementation (our Interpreter backend) could be found here:                glow/lib/Backends/Interpreter/InterpreterNodes.cpp                    Line 40       in       405e632                                                 void Interpreter::fwdConvolutionInst_FloatImpl(Value *inV, Value *outV,                     It has parameters, such as group, pad, stride, filterSize. Convolution is 2D operation (it always works with 2D image and 2D filter, and produces 2D result). Right now all our Convolution implementations assume that pad is the same for both dimensions (image height and width). But for some models (very rarely) it's not true. In general case, there could be 4 different pads: left side, right side, top side, bottom side. We need to change "pad" to be a vector instead of a single number (for ConvolutionNode and ConvolutionInstr). And change all the implementations: Interpreter (float and quantized), CPU (float and quantized). Later, we also need to support uneven paddings in ConvolutionGradNode (which is backward pass for Convolution). Note, that our Convolution for CPU backend is highly optimized, and in theory complicating its code may lead to losing performance. In practice, I highly doubt that this could happen, but worth to check performance after the change just to be sure. One can run tests/images/run.sh -cpu -iterations=100 with and without the change, and make sure that average performance numbers are within 1%. Here is ONNX specification of Conv operator: https://github.com/onnx/onnx/blob/master/docs/Operators.md#conv One can notice that not only padding is represented as array there, but also stride and filterSize are represented as array. Changing these is lower priority, and there's no immediate need. Just good thing to have. Another direction of future work: support non-square padding in PoolMax and PoolAvg operators.

title: Assumptions baked in the Graph optimizer not checked anywhere
author: qcolombet
body: Some of the Graph optimizations assume that some nodes have variables as their inputs (e.g., batch normalization, convolution) and that these variables are used only in those nodes. Although this currently matches what the importers emit, this creates an unwelcome coupling. In essence, we could spot usage of cast<Variable> sprinkled in the code base. We should either:  Check these assumptions in the related verify methods, or Fix the optimizer (and the hand written test cases)  I am tempted to go with #2 because: A. Only the optimizer, importer and test cases have these assumptions baked in (for instance, the CPU optimization for convolution optimizeCPUConv is fine without those, same for the lowering and the interpreter.) B. It is not unlikely that constant Variables with the same value would be uniqued and be shared across different uses and that's never checked. C. With the introduce of the load node, those optimizations will need to be taught how to look through loads anyway.

title: Refactor Backend interface
author: stoklund
body: The glow::Backend interface is current storing a lot of state, and it needs to be refactored. We want to clearly separate the hardware abstraction layer from the different kinds of state we're storing. Over in #1176 we want to compile multiple functions to run on different CPUs. In the future, we also want to support multiple GPUs and other accelerators, so we need a backend interface that separates state related to different functions and different execution units. I'll elaborate on a design in the comments below.

title: Separate HAL, temporary state, and compiled functions
author: stoklund
body: This is part of the Backend refactoring in #1227. The goal is to have the Backend sub-classes represent the hardware abstraction layer. The instances hold no mutable state, and all actions are performed through const virtual functions. Proposed interface: class Backend {   virtual bool transformPreLowering(Function *F, CompilationMode mode) const;   virtual bool transformPostLowering(Function *F, CompilationMode mode) const;   virtual bool isOpSupported(Kinded::Kind opKind, ElemKind elementTy) const;   virtual bool shouldLower(const Node *N) const;   virtual bool shouldShareBuffers() const;    /// Compile an IR function, consuming it in the process.   /// Returns a new object representing the compiled function.   virtual unique_ptr<CompiledFunction> compileFunction(unique_ptr<IRFunction>) const; }  class CompiledFunction {   virtual void execute() =0; } Refactoring steps:  Change transformPreLowering and friends to be const. Create a CompiledFunction sub-class per backend which holds the result of compiling a function. Move remaining temporary compilation state out of the Backend sub-classes into a locally defined class that only exists during compileFunction(). Remove the IRFunction  pointer from backend instances and the createBackend() function.  At this stage, the CompiledFunction sub-classes will still reference the original module, and their execute method can modify variables in the module.

title: shareBuffers fails to merge chain of copies
author: qcolombet
body: As found in #1209, our shareBuffers optimization fails to merge chain of copies. The problem is illustrated with the test case in #1237. Copy/pasting the analysis made in #1209: In a nutshell, our buffer optimization only looks at merging one segment at a time. In the case of the lowering of the load node, we have for the first time potentially more than one copy on a chain to a use (e.g., with the lowering of reshape(load)) . Now to illustrate the problem with chain of copy, let us consider: 1: a = copy b 2: c = copy a 3: = c We have the following segments: a = (1, 2); b = (-,1); c (2, 3) First we merge c and a: 1: a = copy b 2: a = copy a 3: = a Now the segments look like: a = (1, 2), (2, 3); b = (-,1) When considering merging a with b, we only consider updating the segment of a that encloses the segment of b, thus (1,2). The updated code looks like: 1: b = copy b 2: a = copy b 3: = a We don't update the old c segment and end up with a copy in 2 now. Interestingly, if you delete the useless copies as you go, you actually end up with incorrect code, e.g., for the previous example: 1: b = copy b ---2: a = copy b---- deleted 3: = a <--- a never defined This is because when we update the instruction, we don't preserve the last definition of the outgoing variable and given we don't update the uses not in the segment, they potentially reference an undefined variable. It looks like it works just by accident but maybe it was intended this way? Long story short we need to lift the one-segment-at-a-time limitation (maybe by merging the segments?).

title: Graph partitioning for multi-device execution
author: bertmaher
body: Partitioning a Function into multiple subgraphs breaks a lot of assumptions in our current architecture.  PR #1176 shows a proof-of-concept for the mechanics of partitioning, but I want to step back and figure out how this fits into the whole system. Let's consider the interfaces we currently have:  ExecutionEngine is configured with a particular Backend and knows how to compile a Function for it. Once compiled, EE can run a function with particular Variable-to-Tensor bindings. Internally to EE, Backend compiles an IRFunction, creating a CompiledFunction. CompiledFunction can execute itself.  It assumes Tensor bindings are performed externally (but see #1227 for an alternate design).  The main difficulty with partitioning is that it complicates the pipeline: Function->IRFunction->CompiledFunction->execute With partitioning, we have to decide where to split a Function into a DAG of Functions, and how to appropriately propagate the dependence information. Furthermore some of the choices we make will be backend specific.  The following scenarios could apply:  CPU execution in which each part is generated sequentially, and a higher-level Executor manages scheduling of parts onto threads CPU execution in which synchronization is compiled in to the graph Accelerator execution where synchronization generates inter-card DMA operations

title: Wrong scheduling because of the lack of memory dependencies
author: qcolombet
body: Our graph does not model the memory dependencies explicitly. As a result, if we have a variable is written and read on different data paths, the scheduler may be unlucky and we read the wrong version of the variable.  Essentially, if you have:      A     / \ write read  The scheduler can produce either: write A read A or read A write A  Obviously this does not produce the same output. Glow intended semantic is that write should happen last, but with our current algorithm, this is actually possible to fool the scheduler not to do that.  I'm going to send a PR to show how we can fool the scheduler.

title: Should lower/optimize behave differently based on the compilation mode?
author: qcolombet
body: As of today our API takes the CompilationMode for both the lowering and optimization phase (glow::lower and glow::optimize). Except for one thing in the lowering, which I will come back later, this argument does change the behavior of these functions and thus, I was wondering if we should pass it at all. My way of thinking is if we don't use it, let's not pass it and if/when we need it we can add it. Now going back to the only user of this argument in lowering. The lowering of batch normalization is the only user of that argument, but I believe we could avoid that use and that would be a better design. Basically, we lower BN differently between inference and training, whereas I think the right thing would be to have a different representation when we differentiate BN. In essence, what I am suggesting for this use case is to introduce a new node for mean and variance normalization (i.e., for what we special case with the training mode during lowering.) In other words, differentiation for BN would produce BNGrad(BN(meanVarNorm)) and that would completely eliminate the need for a special lowering. All in all, as of today, I don't see a reason why we pass this mode. What do people think?

title: [Broadcasting] Concat inputs scale with the broadcast size.
author: jfix71
body: We represent a broadcast as a series of concats. For example if we want to broadcast a tensor A with dims = {1} to a tensor B with dims = {10}, B is a ConcatNode with A repeatedly input 10 times. This works nicely because we do not need a BroadcastNode. Additionally, we IRGen this ConcatNode with repeated inputs into a single InsertTensorInst with some count value, i.e. the InsertTensorInst does not have its input count scale with the broadcast size. However, this scaling issue does occur at the Node level. If the broadcast size is large, for example if the destination tensor B has  dims = {2048}, then B will be a ConcatNode with 2048 inputs. Not great. To improve this, one option I am considering is to add a vector member to ConcatNode that represents how many times to concatenate each input. For example, instead of the above ConcatNode B having A input 2048 times, it has A input once, as well as a new "count" member vector {2048}, signaling that A should be inserted 2048 times. If we wanted to also Concat some other Node C 10 times at the end, then this "count" member vector would be {2048, 10}, and B would have A and C input once each. This would mean ConcatNode more closely matches our InsertTensorInst, which ConcatNode is IRGen'd into anyway. However, it adds some complexity to the ConcatNode. What does everyone think?

title: [quantization] Add symmetric quantization schema support to Glow
author: rdzhabarov
body: Current state The latest version of Glow compiler provides a certain level of quantization support. Quantization process consists of the following steps:   Instrument an original floating-point graph with the special Quantization Profile node   Run inference on the instrumented graph many times with good representative inputs (see dump_profile flag). During this step Glow automatically captures the distribution of all activations in the compute graph. The distribution contains min/max value seen from the given output of the graph node as well as detailed frequency per floating point range withing [min, max] interval. There are 2000 floating point ranges kept as part of the Quantization Profile node. As the result of the profiling procedure, Glow generates Scale and Offset parameters for all activations and dumps it in the file (Note, currently Glow uses linear quantization). The scale is a positive fp32 number while Offset is an int32. Note, Glow does not use the distribution of floating point numbers but relies only on values of min and max (this is a separate issue and out of scope here).   Transform computation graph based on the captured profile and specific execution backend. Note, not all nodes are quantized as not all backends support certain quantized op. See CPU backend op support here for example.   Perform computation of quantized graph. See Interpreter implementation here.   What needs to be enhanced There are backends that tight to a specific quantization schema, e.g., symmetric quantization. The difference between symmetric and assymetric quantization is that the "offset" parameter equals to 0 in symmetric linear quantization. In this case the dequantization follows the formula: fp32_number = scale * quantized_number (fp32_number = scale * (quantized_number - offset) for the asymmetric case). Requirement for the symmetric quantization  Need to make sure that the accuracy loss is comparable with the asymmetric case on Resnet50. Important note, currently, activations are signed int8 and in case of symmetric quantization, outputs of Sigmoid/ReLU will effectively use only 7 bits out of 8 (which is undesirable).  The issue could be tackled in two steps:  Introduce the symmetric schema and deal with the int8 activations (accuracy loss) Introduce int8, uint8 activations. Check if specific backend can handle int8/uint8 activations for a given Op (this way we could gradually onboard backends). This is a bigger change and would require a design discussion here.  Please discuss this issue here before implementation. cc: @qcolombet

title: Add support for FP16 and bfloat
author: stoklund
body: Working with accelerators, we are going to need support for 16-bit floating point types.  FP16 is the binary16 format defined in IEEE 754-2008. bfloat is the Tensorflow floating point type with the same exponent range as a float.     Type binary16 bfloat binary32     k, storage width in bits 16 16 32   w, exponent field width in bits 5 8 8   t, trailing significand field width in bits 10 7 23    We should at a minimum add these types to glow::ElemKind so we can represent low-precision tensors in these types. Ideally, also add interpreter support.

title: Need to redesign the Variable interface.
author: nadavrot
body: Motivation Currently Glow variables are backed by Tensors, and are tied to the graph. This gives us the ability to perform optimizations such as constant propagation that mutate the content of Tensors. However, it also ties the input/output tensors to the module. This design prevents us from running multithreaded programs simply because the input/output variables (which need to be different for each thread) are a single entity. Proposed design The proposed solution is to separate the concept of symbolic variables from graph variables. For example, an input variable X will not be backed by a Tensor until the execution-engine executes the compiled program. To execute the network the caller would need to bind Tensors to variables. The execution engine actually already does this, so we won't need to change the APIs that are used by our unit tests. To preserve the ability to perform constant propagation (and other tensor-content optimizations) we would need to be able to make some variables concrete during the compilation phase. We would need to have two kinds of variables: Constant - this is a tensor-backed variable. Similar to LLVM's ConstantArray it's a data structure that lives at the module-level and can be manipulated by transformations. Variable - this is a typed variable that isn't backed by a real tensor until runtime. The runtime allocates the tensor (either in device memory or on the host) and manages the input/output to and from the variable.

title: Our def-use chains are counter intuitive (and error-prone IMHO)
author: qcolombet
body: When we have nodes with several outputs (like TopK or MeanVarNormalization), we don't track the def-use chain per output but instead we do it per node. In effect, imagine we have something like: auto *topK = createTopK auto *values = topK.getValues(); auto *indices = topK.getIndices(); Walking the users for all three variables will give us the exact same def-use chain. So for instance, walking through the users of indices and doing some changes without checking that the use is of the right NodeValue (i.e., checking that the ResNos are the same) will produce incorrect code. Another instance is checking hasOneUse for values could be false because indices could also be used. replaceAllUsesOfWith does the right thing, but one would expect that the number of updates that function does is equal to the number of users the related value has. Right now, it is not the case. This bit me when I was writing some asserts where I thought the NodeValue would have one use. I'll write a test case to show the issue.

title: [Quantization] Profile and Quantize components Nodes of lowered Nodes
author: jfix71
body: Right now we do profiling on the graph prior to lowering. I will use FullyConnected nodes as a running example. They are lowered into a MatMul and BatchedAdd node. However the FullyConnected nodes have only their output profiled, meaning the output of the last node (BatchedAdd). This means we do not have profiling information about the MatMul, and we are forced to use the profile from the BatchedAdd for the MatMul when lowering the quantized FullyConnected node. This means we could lose some precision unnecessarily. We could instead lower all nodes prior to profiling. We would then get profiles for both the MatMul and BatchedAdd. This way we do not lose any information about the components of the lowered FullyConnected node. After profiling we load this profile information back in for quantization, which now includes all component node's profiles. At this point, one option to proceed is to apply quantization to the unlowered graph based on the lowered component profiles (e.g. still quantize the FullyConnected node using the BatchedAdd profile). This could be necessary because we currently quantize prior to compiling, which is where we do optimizations and lowering. We would then need to additionally keep track of each unlowered node's component node's quantization parameters, so that we can use these parameters when the nodes are lowered (e.g. make sure when we lower the quantized FullyConnected node we can find and use its component MatMul node's quantization parameters). So it seems we would need to create a map from unlowered nodes to their lowered component profiles/quantization parameters, e.g. map from the FullyConnected Node to the BatchedAdd and MatMul profiles/quantization parameters. This map would need to be passed into lower(). I believe other options would require a redesign of the order in which we apply quantization vs. optimizations and lowering.

title: Graph optimizer should perform constant folding
author: opti-mix
body: If e.g. both operands of an arithmetic operation like add or sub are splats (i.e. constants) or more generally tensors with payloads statically known at compile-time , the result of the operation can be computed at compile-time. The process of evaluation the constant expressions at compile time is known as constant folding. Such constant computations may arise e.g. after applying some other optimizations or transformations. Currently, Glow's graph optimizer does not support constant folding. But it should be fairly easy to extend the graph optimizer to support constant folding. Most likely it should be performed during the execution of simplifyNode in GraphOptimizer.cpp

title: [RFC] Softmax quantization problematic
author: tlepley-cadence
body: When adding the support for Softmax quantization, I ran into an issue due to the fact that  the Softmax node is declared as propagating  the input type to the output The Softmax instruction checks that the input type is equal to the output type In Glow, the scale/offset are part of the tensor type  With our model, the quantization profile scale is substantially different between the input and the output (input scale = 0.245214, out scale = 0.00682523). Having the input scale propagated to the output makes the quantized Softmax generate only 0 in many cases. Here, this is really a scale issue and adding a RescaleQuantized node after Softmax to match the profile scale, like it's done for MaxPooling for instance, would not help (requantizing 0 will still gives 0) I'd like to have your opinion for the best approach to take. Maybe the main source of the problem is that the scale/offset information is in Type. If it was moved out of Type, I think it would solve many problem swe are going to encounter as we add more nodes that support quantization. In the meantime, the workaround I implemented was to change the declaration of both Softmax node and instruction (see  PR #1511). Summary:  declare .addResultFromCtorArg() for the node declaration remove  .inplaceOperand({"Dest", "Src"}) and  .autoVerify(VerifyKind::SameType, {"Dest", "Src"}) for the instruction declaration I also had to add a more relaxed Type equality checking method. Since scale/offset are part of the Type objects, the isEqual methods is in some situation a bit too strict. Sometimes, we just want to check that the shape and the element types are equal, not the scale/offset.

title: [RFC] Error reporting, malformed graph, and general resilience
author: qcolombet
body: Context Glow checks are for the most part bound to whether or not asserts are enabled in the build. The rationale is we expect the inputs (network, weights) to be correctly shaped and sized when we invoke the compiler/loaders and thus this design eliminates unnecessary overhead. Problems Given most checks are removed in release mode, we end up in a situation where we cannot use this variant when bringing up new works. For instance, silly mistakes like shaping incorrectly a transpose will produce random compiler errors or just invalid/inaccurate outputs with no way to tell what is going wrong. Then, running the same network with a debug variant would trigger a verifier failure from the beginning, hinting directly at what the problem was. This process is far from being intuitive and is cumbersome. In essence, we have the following problems:  The debug mode gives us diagnostics but is slow to run. The release mode is fast to run but does not gives any information on what is going on. The error reporting through asserts has too little context to be actionable on its own.  To make a comparison, Glow behaves like a compiler that wouldn't issue a syntax error diagnostic if compiled with assert disabled. On top of that, when the assertions are enabled, errors like type mismatch would be reported bluntly: no location in the source file, no naming of the type that was causing the problem and so on. In a nutshell, when working on a new model, the process may look like this:  Run the network with the release variant => compiler crashes Run the network with the debug variant => assertion failure "invalid..." Run the network with the debug variant in a debugger => assertion failure "invalid...", then print variables, examine the memory, etc. to see what is wrong.  Finally, for large networks, it is possible that the debug mode is too slow to be practical, making debugging very hard. Ultimate Goal Ideally, we would like to be sure that only valid IR hit the compiler. Then, in the compiler itself, it seems reasonable to rely on asserts for things related to the IR, like the invariants after such and such optimizations and so on. Indeed, at this point, any problem occurring in the compiler is the result of a wrong doing of the compiler itself and thus not actionable by the user. Of course, we would still need to have some kind of non-assert based error reporting for anything that is not in the control of the compiler. E.g., failing to write to the filesystem, out-of-memory allocation, network too big for the targeted backend, etc. How Do We Get There? We basically have two approaches to make sure only valid IR hit the compiler:  Have every "frontend" of Glow performs the checks (e.g., like the protobuf loaders). Have Glow performs the checks before doing anything.  The second approach would be the preferred way as it focused the burden of validating the IR in only one place. However, this potentially makes error reporting more difficult for the backends. Therefore, we likely would want both. Regarding the general error reporting, I believe we would want to have the front-end to register a diagnostic handler in Glow, so that the reporting is properly plumbed there. This is less critical than ensuring that the IR is valid as most users's errors should be caught by the front-end itself. What About Getting Rid of the Unnecessary Checks Then? With the proposed approach, we don't really have a way to get rid of the checks that valid the IR, so how do we avoid to waste resources when we are running for the same network over and over? We see two possible directions here:  Something higher level of Glow, could cache the result of the compilation and such, then it wouldn't invoke Glow or its front-end/loader again and again and instead would directly run what it already had. We could feature a "reckless" mode that effectively disable every error reporting in both the front-end and Glow. This mode wouldn't be the default like it is right now.  For #2, the idea would be that only trusted networks would be run. This could be checked for instance with a whitelist embedded in the compiler/loader. What do people think? cc: @nadavrot, @artemrakhov, @opti-mix, @stoklund, @jfix71, @rdzhabarov, @hegemanjwh2, @beicy, @bertmaher, @tlepley.

title: [ONNXIFI] Execute onnxRunGraph async
author: rdzhabarov
body: ONNXIFI interface specifies that onnxRunGraph should be executed async, see here for details. ONNXIFI_PUBLIC ONNXIFI_CHECK_RESULT onnxStatus ONNXIFI_ABI onnxRunGraph(onnxGraph graph, const onnxMemoryFenceV1 *inputFence,              onnxMemoryFenceV1 *outputFence) Specifically, we should do the following sequence of actions:  Do the checks against type of the syncronization event and tags (it's already handled on the current master) Init output event (this event is used by the caller to track whether current inference has completed or still in progress). Schedule run of this particular inference on a separate thread or thread pool (could be improved down the road) Return ONNXIFI_STATUS_SUCCESS from the onnxRunGraph On the async path of inference execution wait for the input event to fire (this signals that inputs are copied to the proper addresses, which are set on the prior SetGraphIO call) Run inference normally and copy outputs to the required addresses (addresses are specified in the prior SetGraphIO call)  cc: @Maratyszcza @yinghai

title: [RFC] Replace MatMul with BatchMatMul
author: qcolombet
body: TL;DR I suggest to replace MatMul with BatchMatMul, the semantic would be: Inputs [b0,..., bx, m, k], [b0,...,bx, k, n] Output: [b0, ..., bx, m, n] We currently expand Batched matmul operators into a bunch of matmul operators with slicing, reshape and concats. One of the main drawback from this representation is a bloat of the number of operators ending up in the IR and the underlying issue of compile time, memory consumption, hard to analysis sequences to name a few. Instead, I would suggest to replace our matmul operator with a batched matmul operator. Indeed, matmuls are just a special case of a batch of 1. Using this kind of representation would give each backend the freedom to unroll or use loops to realize the expected sequence. Moreover, it would make the modeling of predication more natural, instead of having to do the same gymnastic with slicing and the kind.

title: Currently using floats for Select, CmpEQ, CmpLTE
author: jfix71
body: Right now we are using FloatTy for Variables that are used as the Condition input to Select, when it really should be some sort of boolean/predicate type. Similarly our Interpreter backend creates outputs from CmpEQ/CmpLTE as float. This likely needs to be redesigned with some sort of boolean or predicate ElemKind. One option could be to do this with a generic (no width-specified) ElemKind::PredicateTy. The idea here is to allow the backend to implement it with whatever bit width it wants. One issue is that Variables have their ElemKind specified independently of a backend/prior to picking or setting the backend. So we would need to allocate the tensors backing these Variables with some specific size prior to knowing what size the backend we are running with would like to use. The backend would need to convert them to the size the backend prefers. Another option could be to add something like ElemKind::Predicate8Ty, where the bit width is explicit. The width would stay static and we could allocate tensors backing Variables with this width as such. Backends could still change the size of the predicate if they wanted once the Instruction level IR reaches it, i.e. in Backend::compile(). Either way it does seem we will need the backend to massage the type to fit its internal representation. So in some sense these are different flavors of the same thing; e.g. if we used 8 as the default width for for the ElemKind::PredicateTy option it seems almost identical to just using ElemKind::Predicate8Ty.

title: [RFC] Perform deeper function cloning. Some variables needs to be cloned.
author: rdzhabarov
body: Usage of cloning function Glow currently provides a convenience method to clone an existing high level IR Function. This functionality is used for procedures like:  Profile quantization Quantization Differentiation  Cloning semantics The semantics of cloning is to create a new Function with all nodes cloned (basically, creating a new nodes) and restore edges in the new Function based on the original one. Cloning does not involve cloning variables in any way, so that newly cloned Function reuses the same variables as the original one. Multiple writers issue At the moment of inference some of the variables are read only variables like weights while others (e.g., connected to the Save node) are not. Having Save nodes clonned while sharing variables creates a situation when results of inference on one function overwrites results of inference on another function. This feels like an unexpected behavior when normally cloning is done with copy on write or just cloning shared resource. Currently, quantization end to end test does not perform any sensible validation as second inference run overwrites original values. Options to fix this  The most natural way is to let Node cloning method to decide what needs to be cloned. Currently, it's just node itself, but for the case of Save node it could clone the output variable first and use that to create a new Save node. Let the cloning procedure to handle variables and clone some of them. This way cloning procedure needs somehow to know whether var is output var and clone only those. Other options?  @qcolombet, you looked at Save nodes a lot in the past. What do you think?

title: Implement a method to convert Placeholder to Constant
author: nadavrot
body: Once we eliminate all mutable variables we'll be left with Placeholders that could be bound to specific Tensors by the Context, and to Constants, that are owned by the graph. The optimizer is only allowed to optimize Constants, because the Placeholders are observable by the outside world and must not be mutated. To enable optimizations we need to implement a method that takes a Graph and some context and turn some Placeholders into constants. For example, consider the trained mnist graph. After training the program and before running inference it could be a good idea to convert all of the weights (but not the inputs and outputs) into constants. This would allow the optimizer to touch and mutate the constants and generate better code. One possible signature: makePlaceholderConstant(Context &ctx, Function * F, llvm::ArrayRef<Placeholder*> vars);

title: Optimization pipeline design with more backend control
author: jfix71
body: Right now we have target-independent optimizations that may or may not benefit the backend executing the graph, and may even degrade performance. We need to allow the backend we are targeting have more control over what optimizations are performed. For example, the GraphOptimizer's small matrix multiplication/batched add merging optimizations (mergeMatMul()/mergeBatchedAdd()) may not be beneficial (#1494). Another example is the GraphOptimizer's optimizePool(), where we swap RELU -> MaxPool to MaxPool -> RELU. If the original subgraph is Conv -> RELU -> MaxPool, backends may prefer to vertically fuse Conv -> RELU into a single ConvRELU instead of  swapping the order of the RELU and MaxPool. So this optimization might be counterproductive/may prevent fusion from occurring. Also related to #1633.

title: [RFC] Provide a concise and readable textual representation for the Glow Graph
author: arnabde03
body: Graph optimization unit tests in Glow requires the user to create the input Graph using C++ API which can be quite verbose, unintuitive and error-prone. A textual representation that is easy to read and write would help in writing unit tests and inspecting a Graph. Example of an Graph optimization test written using C++ API In the following example, an input Graph is created using C++ API and passed to the optimize call. TEST_F(GraphOptz, optimizeBatchNormAfterConv) {   Node *A = mod_.createVariable(ElemKind::FloatTy, {1, 10, 20, 3}, "A",                                  VisibilityKind::Public, false);   Node *CV = F_->createConv("conv", A, 16, 5, 1, 2, 1);   Node *BN = F_->createBatchNormalization("batch", CV, 3, 0.0001, 0.9);   F_->createSave("ret", BN);    EXPECT_EQ(F_->getNodes().size(), 3);    ::glow::optimize(F_, CompilationMode::Infer);   EXPECT_EQ(F_->getNodes().size(), 2); } Proposed textual representation of the input Graph and the corresponding unit test @A = public <1 x 10 x 20 x 3>float zero  function @fct() {   %conv = conv input:@A, depth:16, kernel:5, stride:1, pad:2, group:1   %batch = batchnorm input:%conv, channel:3, epsilon:0.0001, momentum:0.9:float   %ret = save input:%batch  }  Global variables start with @, local variables start with %. A global variable declaration specifies the name of the variable, its type, visibility and initial value. A function is a sequence of "operation" nodes. Each node specifies its kind, has a list of named and optionally typed inputs and an optional output. The unit test described in the previous section looks like the following: TEST_F(GraphOptz, optimizeBatchNormAfterConv) {   std::istream is = ... //read the input from a file/string   readGraph(mod_, is);   EXPECT_EQ(F_->getNodes().size(), 3);    ::glow::optimize(F_, CompilationMode::Infer);   EXPECT_EQ(F_->getNodes().size(), 2); }  EBNF Grammar for textual representation of a Glow Graph <var_name> = <global_var_name> | <local_var_name> <value> = <var_name> | <constant> <scalar_type> = 'i32' | 'float' | ... <tensor_type> = '<'<int_constant> {'X' <int_constant>} '>' <scalar_type> <type> = <scalar_type> | <tensor_type> <op_node> = <var_name> '=' <op_name> {<input_name>':'<value>[':'<type>]} <function> = 'function '<function_name> '{' {<op_node>} '}' <visibility> = 'private' | 'public' <initial_value> = 'zero' | 'xavier' <global_var_node> = <global_var_name> '=' <visibility> <type> <initial_value> <module> = {<global_var_node>} {<function>}  Omitted some grammar rules such as <op_name> that are obvious in this context.

title: [GraphOptimizer] Optimizations clobber graph with dead nodes
author: aturetsk
body: Optimizations in GLOW do not erase transformed nodes from the graph and relay on DCE to clean up. This corrupts number of node users (e.g. an optimization can't relay on node->hasOneUser() unless DCE has been done right before it). It looks like GLOW optimizations are going to be refactored into separate classes inherited from FunctionPass (#1659). In this case one of the possible solutions is to make FunctionPass class always call DCE after the optimization is done.

title: Replace llvm::iplist<Instruction> with TaggedList<Instruction> in IRFunction
author: stoklund
body: I want to introduce a new linked list data structure, TaggedList. This is an intrusive doubly linked list like llvm::iplist with the following differences:  Each node has a uint32_t tag member. These tags are maintained online in a strictly increasing order. This means that the relative position of elements in the list can be determined in (fast) constant time, even while inserting and removing elements from the list. The list has a constant time size() operation, maintained as a member in the TaggedList class. This is needed for the online tag maintenance algorithm. Splicing is a linear time operation because the new elements need to be tagged correctly. This is already the case for our specialization of transferNodesFromList(). The tag also makes it possible to detect when an end() iterator is dereferenced or incremented.  I have implemented a prototype of TaggedList based on the Two simplified algorithms for maintaining order in a list paper in order to run benchmarks. List insertions are O(log N) with excellent constant factors. We already have class LiveIntervalsInstructionNumbering in IROptimizer.cpp. This change makes that class redundant by providing the same functionality while also allowing online instruction insertions. The online instruction ordering is needed to implement advanced memory allocation and scheduling in backends. Preemptively Answered Questions:  No, we can't extend llvm::iplist with this functionality because a) iplist::size() is linear time, and b) despite using 27 template classes for configuration and specialization, iplist doesn't offer the hooks needed. No, we can't implement this as a hack in IRFunction because a) we need the constant time size() operator, and b) IRFunction::getInstrs() exposes the list implementation, and we can't prevent users from modifying the list and invalidating our side tables.

title: Remove all executable tests from the Caffe2 and ONNX loaders
author: nadavrot
body: The role of the Caffe2 and ONNX loaders is to load the protobuf from a protobuf file into the Glow graph. The loader unit tests need to check that the complex operators are loaded into the graph nodes properly and that the correct graph is constructed. The operator unit tests need to verify that the low-level operators are executed correctly. Some of the loaders create a complex structure of nodes, but this design is not ideal for a number of reasons.  First, the same structure has to be duplicated between the ONNX and Caffe2 loaders, or shared by means of inheritance. Second, the unit tests that check the loader become complex and slow. A better design would be to use the graph builder to generate the non trivial nodes. To demonstrate this PR let's look at the transposed-matmul node. The loader needs to construct the two nodes: transpose + matmul. These nodes are already tested independently in the operator unit test. A clean implementation and unit test would be to add a graph builder that creates the new construct, that looks like createTransposedMatmul(). We could write an operator test for the createTransposedMatmul method, if we feel like it is complex enough to be worth a unit test. The c2/onnx loader just needs to call createTransposedMatmul, and the unit test just needs to verify that the two nodes are created. The Loader unit test should not execute any networks, they are unit tests, not system tests. In this task you will need to go over the caffe2 unit tests and identify the new operators. Refactor each new complex operator inside the loader into the 'createXXX' method, and move the execution part of the unit test into a new test in the operator test unit test.

title: Tracking of quantization parameters lacks granularity
author: qcolombet
body: Right now, the TensorQuantizationParams only tracks one type per NodeValue, whereas we would need one type for the output and one for each user of that value. E.g., for val = node = use1 val = use2 val  We would want to track independently the types for the result of node, the use of val in use1, and the use of val in use2, in respectively outTy, inTy1, and inTy2, so that we can generate: outTy = node inTy1 = cast outTy = use1 inTy1 inTy2 = cast outTy = use2 inTy2  But instead what we track only one type like this: outTy = node = use1 outTy = use2 outTy  However, sometimes outTy is not suitable for the input and sometimes, the outTy is not suitable for the output itself! What this means basically is outTy encodes the inTy constraints whereas they may disagree. This happens for cases where for instance, the quantized parameters for the output have a different scale than the input, whereas the operation itself doesn't allow that. E.g., the constraints for outTy = op inTy are outTy == inTy, but the quantization profiling gave different types to outTy and inTy. To be more concrete here, LocalResponseNormalizationNode is one such node: the quantization of the output type may have different parameters of the quantization of the input type. I am not sure if we need to fix the tracking of the quantization parameters or if we need to relax the type constraints on those operators. E.g., do we really need LocalResponseNormalizationNode to have the same scale and offset for its input and output, I am not sure. Perhaps we want to fix the verifier to check that the element type and dimensions are the same. Or maybe we want both! (the finer granularity and the relaxed verifier check) @rdzhabarov what do you think?

title: [Quantization] Interpreter quantization should approximate realistic backend quantization
author: jfix71
body: Currently the Interpreter's quantization implementation uses floating point arithmetic in many places to ensure that we do not lose precision (see fwdElementAddInst_I8Impl() as an example). This is different than what we see in our CPU backend, and what we expect to see in other backends/accelerators -- floating point arithmetic is avoided as much as possible. Given that the Interpreter is supposed to be a reference for the other backends, I believe it makes more sense for the Interpreter to follow other backends here, and not use floating point arithmetic to improve its quantization accuracy. I have created a test case in OperatorTest on my fork that displays the issue, where the CPU Backend fails a test that the Interpreter test passes, because the Interpreter test has better accuracy.

title: Pass Context at runtime not compile time
author: gcatron
body: In order to facilitate multi-threaded execution context passing needs to be moved from compile time to runtime.  This will break the current API! At compile time, constant weight allocation will remain unchanged, however Placeholder memory will no longer be allocated at runtime. The expected sizes will be calculated from the the Placeholder types. At runtime (ExecutionEngine::run) the context will be passed in and Placeholder memory will be assigned to point to the allocations in the context. When done context will no longer be a parameter of the compile function. ExecutionEngine::run and function::execute will expect a context parameter. This change will be done in stages to minimize disruption.   ExecutionEngine::run(Context &ctx) will be introduced. This is the new execution flow. When the bugs are worked out it will replace run. Tests will be ported to use run(ctx).   CompiledFunction::execute(Context &ctx) will be introduced, similar to run(ctx) this will replace execute() when the work is finished. Tests will be ported to execute(Context &ctx).   execute(Context &ctx) will be updated to handle memory allocation at runtime.   Once runctx and execute(ctx) are working and all tests pass run(ctx) will replace run and execute(ctx) will replace execute. At this point any external code will need to be updated to reflect these changes.

title: [ImageClassifier] Broken `-convert-inout-to-fp16` due to recent refactoring
author: qcolombet
body: TL;DR We need to do the conversion from fp32 to fp16 of the data tensor (load image) after we compile not before. When we landed #1910 we missed a subtle difference in the order we do things that leads to broken graphs when using -convert-inout-to-fp16 alone for the image-classifier. Basically, -convert-inout-to-fp16 is responsible for changing the input and output placeholder from float32 to float16 and for inserting the proper convert nodes in the graph. When this conversion sees a placeholder with already the right type, it does nothing as it should. So far so good. This refactoring however changed the type of the input placeholder before running the conversion has been done, thus we end up with the placeholder wrongly typed and the conversion thinks things are fine. When you look at the code itself, it's hard to see at first glance what we did differently. The old order look like:  Load the input data Create the loader Convert the input data from fp32 to fp16 Convert the input placeholder from fp32 to fp16 Compiling the network Running  The new order swapped 2 <-> 3:  Load the input data Convert the input data from fp32 to fp16 Create the loader Convert the input placeholder from fp32 to fp16 Compiling the network Running  This is problematic because the loader actually uses the type of the input tensor data to create the placeholder and thus it thinks the network is already fp16 ready and that's the bug. The challenge with the refactoring is that 2, 4, 5 needs to happen only once, whereas 3 needs to happen at each run. We decided to move it right after 1, whereas we actually need to move it just before 6. To reproduce, just build image-classifier with asserts enabled use resnet50 (for instance) and -convert-inout-to-fp16 and the verifier should assert.

title: Issue with padding ?

In particular, the Glow code assumes that padding in the model is just given for spatial dimensions (array of 4 numbers), while ONNX specifies that the padding should be given for all dimensions (array of 8 values for a 4D tensor):  The value represent the number of pixels added to the beginning and end part of the corresponding axis. pads format should be as follow [x1_begin, x2_begin...x1_end, x2_end,...], where xi_begin the number of pixels added at the beginning of axis i and xi_end, the number of pixels added at the end of axis i.  I would like to make sure that we all agree on the interpretation of the ONNX spec, even if we decide for now that we just want to support spatial padding in Glow. For instance, if we want to grow the tensor spatially, the 'pads' attribute in the model would be (considering NCHW) : [ 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1] , and not [1, 1, 1, 1] Any opinion ?

title: ONNXIFI BackendIDs and Backends
author: yinghai

In offline discussion, we agreed that we should have one copy of backendIDs while creating as many backends as we want as a view into the backends. But this creates several problems due to the fact that we one have one ExecutionEngine in the backend:  Thread safety when accessing anything about ExecutionEngine Check compatibility and run graph is going to be slow as they will be serialized. A minor problem that we now compile every ONNXIFI module into function with the same name.  Some idea: Can we have a pool of ExecutionEngines in the BackendID, and every time we create a backend from that backendID, we give it an ArrayRef of these EEs? When we compile a graph,  we hash the mode model id to pick one of the EEs to use. Access to the engines should be protected by locks. And we compile functions with the name inference_graphID.

title: [Quantization] Leave the decision of forcing the output scale/offset to be the same as the input to backends.
author: beicy
body: In our previous quantization procedure, we forced the following type of quantized node output have the same quantization param as the input: Kinded::Kind::LocalResponseNormalizationNodeKind                        Kinded::Kind::SliceNodeKind                                       Kinded::Kind::ReshapeNodeKind                                        Kinded::Kind::TopKNodeKind                                         Kinded::Kind::GatherNodeKind                                          Kinded::Kind::MaxPoolNodeKind  However, as @tlepley-cadence suggested,  since it is generally an accuracy vs speed tradeoff that  should be left to the backend designer. We would like to evaluate those ops, and leave some or all of the decision to backends.

title: Manage tensors in model loaders as unique_ptrs instead of raw pointers
author: jackm321
body: Now that the model loaders have error handling, memory that they allocate must be handled with care and cleaned up when an error occurs or there could be a leak (there was already one). To make managing the memory allocated for tensors more robust in the face of errors, we should use llvm::StringMap<std::unique_ptr<Tensor>> tensors_ instead of llvm::StringMap<Tensor *> tensors_ in ProtobufLoader. Any loader inheriting from ProtobufLoader should allocate all tensors as unique_ptrs and move them to tensors_ to avoid leaks.

title: Non unique naming for instructions
author: jsubag

I've found a case where this caused two instructions to have the same name. One way to fix it would be by replacing it with: os << "  auto *V = builder_.create" << name_ << "Inst(N->getName()";  And remove                glow/tools/ClassGen/InstrBuilder.cpp                    Line 406       in       ad7c0f8                                                 os << "  V->setName(N->getName());\n";

title: [RFC] isOpSupported() redesign?
author: jfix71
body: I'm not sure the isOpSupported() API makes sense as currently specified -- I think backends need to decide if an op is supported based on the expected precision of all inputs and outputs. Perhaps the API should take in the Node itself and not the Kind+ElemKind. That way the backend can look at all of the node's inputs/outputs. Additionally, for backends that use the Instruction-level IR, I think we should consider adding a pass over the final Instructions with another version of isOpSupported() for Instructions. It's possible for a bug to exist during the compilation phases (lowering to other Nodes, and then lowering via IRGen, and many graph/instruction optimization passes) that results in the final Instruction list not being supported by the backend. This should be caught as early as possible during compilation and return a compilation error up the stack.

title: Codegen of FullyConnected (via ONNXIFI) is really suboptimal

title: Separate Code Generation and Constant Collection during Compile
author: gcatron
body: Background: With the new runtime design (#2045) we split the compilation step into two parts parts, code generation and collecting constants. Code generation is when the graph is converted to executable code that will run on the platform. Collecting Constants is the process of gathering weights and constants from the input module and copying them into a single chunk of memory for execution and copying to the device. Impact: This means we need to introduce a new method to the Backend interface. Namely, compileWithoutConstants. This does everything compile does except collect constants to one region of memory.

title: [RFC] Can we remove transformPreLowering()?
author: jfix71
body: The original intent of transformPreLowering() was to allow for a backend to transform the graph before lowering makes it potentially much harder to understand the higher-level structure of the graph and perform preferred transformations. However, we later added shouldLower() to allow a backend to prevent such problematic lowering. This means that instead of using transformPreLowering(), the backend can prevent lowering of nodes via shouldLower(), and then do its preferred transformations during transformPostLowering(). So, some motivations here to remove transformPreLowering():  I'm not sure any of our backends are using this functionality given the ability to prevent lowering via shouldLower(). Simplify the compilation pipeline if it's not clearly useful. Once #2311 lands, when quantizing we will be lowering prior to transformPreLowering() anyway, so it's a misleading function and could cause bugs and/or confusion.

title: [unittests] Cannot assume fp32 support on all backends
author: jfix71
body: The OperatorTests below compare reduced precision results (fp16 or quantized) to fp32 results. These tests get the fp32 result from the backend that is being tested, but the backend may not support fp32. The fp32 result should instead be evaluated on the Interpreter. We can probably refactor compareAgainstInterpreter() from BackendCorrectnessTest.cpp in order to automatically do this. This would also allow us to avoid explicitly picking quantization parameters which we do in some of these tests. The flow would be (1) instrument profile the graph; (2) compile/run on the interpreter, gathering the fp32 result along with the quantization profile; (3) quantize the graph using that profile; (4) compile/run on the backend, gathering the reduced precision result to compare against the fp32 result from the interpreter. Edit: Looks like we're doing something like this already in testQuantizationEnd2End(). title: Move the reusable parts of CPUBackend into a LLVMCodeGen library
author: opti-mix
body: As more Glow backends are being developed,  some of them need to directly generate code using LLVM for different targets and architectures. Thus it would be nice if it would be possible to reuse some of the CPUBackend functionalities (e.g. most of LLVMIRGen, bundle saving, may be JIT parts), but with certain backend-specific adjustments. Glow's CPUBackend is not implemented as a reusable component though. For one, all of the implementation is hidden inside this backend's subdirectory and not visible by other backends. Then, in certain places this backend mixes a rather target independent code with x86/CPU-specific code. It may be interesting to decouple the reusable parts of the CPUBackend into a reusable LLVMCodeGen library, so that concrete backends can derive from it and add any backend specific functionality and adjustments. Other possible alternatives, which are less cleaner solutions IMHO:  Extend the CPUBackend with additional logic required by the specific backend. This would essentially result in a situation where we have multiple backends under lib/Backends/CPUBackend. Copy most of the CPUBackend into your new backend subdirectory and adjust it to your liking, which would lead to a lot of code duplication between the new backend and the CPUBackend.

title: FunctionQuantizer silently skipping quantizing nodes
author: jfix71
body: Right now the FunctionQuantizer silently skips quantizing a node if the target backend does not support the quantization precision being converted to (checked via Backend::isOpSupported()). Instead it leaves the node in fp32 and wraps it with dequantize/quantize nodes. Due to this, I've noticed that some of our unit tests that are intended to test precision of quantized graphs are instead just wrapping many of the graph's nodes with dequantize/quantize. This kind of defeats the purpose of the test. A couple examples are QuantizationTest's JIT/Operator.end2endInt16/0 and OpenCL/Operator.end2endGRU/0. We've also had occasional regressions where nodes previously quantized no longer were, requiring later fixes, e.g. #2436. Instead, I think we should at least have an option for the FunctionQuantizer to report quantization failure up the stack if the target backend does not support a node it is trying to quantize. If a test or model expects a NodeKind to not be quantized, we already have doNotQuantizeKinds which can be used to prevent the FunctionQuantizer from returning failure in such cases and explicitly allow for specific NodeKinds to stay unquantized. Another option could be to remove this isOpSupported() check in the FunctionQuantizer entirely, and then after quantization check if the graph is supported by the backend. However this is a bit more drastic. We could still use doNotQuantizeKinds in this case though, and this would probably mean we could remove NodeInfo from isOpSupported() (seen in #2235).

title: Folding vs Lowering: improving the compiler flow
author: tlepley-cadence
body: The problematic is the following:  input models (ONNX for instance) can express the exact same functionality with various forms. Examples are LeakyRelu and BatchNorm that may be expressed as a sub-graph rather than a single node in the input model (We've got this situation multiple times) Backend may or may not support a high-level node. This should be handled by the lowering phase that is under their control.  @artemrakhov  proposes in #2613 (for LeakyRelu) to have have a high level operator lowered directly in the high level IR, before lowering, and then to request backends to fold high-level nodes when they support high level function natively (then to do highering after lowering). I don't think this approach should be followed. My proposal is actually to do the opposite: have the high-level IR as high-level as possible and let the lowering pass perform the IR lowering, as expected, driven by backends. There are IMO many advantages:  The high level IR more canonical, what simplifies many optimizations. Another example is for instance BatchNorm that we have often seen unfolded in various ways in converted ONNX models. it makes the compiler flow more consistent, going from high level (high abstraction) to low (level/low abstraction), stage after stage. it simplifies backends and make the high-level IR more independent from the CPU backend specificities. Many backends will support high-level nodes natively, on the contrary to the CPU backend. it make the IR more consistent. Today, for instance, we have Relu in the high IR, so it looks consistent to have LeakyRelu too.  A solution that is IMO clean consists of splitting the glow::optimize() in 2 parts: 1/ IR 'legalizer' called only once at the beginning of the compiler flow. The purpose is to make the high level IR more independent from the input models variants. 2/ Generic optims (sink, merge etc...) called before and after lowering like today. Then, we would have as compiler flow: 1- import model 2- legalize the IR (fold high-level nodes as much as possible) 3- generic optims (no folding) 4- lowering 5- generic optims (no folding)

title: Supporting out-of-process compilation for LLVMBackend-based backends
author: opti-mix
body: Some users have reported about situations where they cannot use LLVM in-processs as a library to compile LLVM bitcode for their respective targets. It may happen e.g. if they work on a new HW and LLVM support for this target is either provided as a closed-source by 3rd party companies or they use customized versions of LLVM which are not 100% compatible with the version used to build Glow. To overcome these troubles, these users asked if it would be possible to support out-of-process compilations for LLVMBackend-based backends. In these scenarios, Glow would still produce the LLVM bitcode as usual, but then it would invoke an external LLVM compiler (llc?) to compile this bitcode into an object file. To support such a feature, we'd need to slightly extend the LLVMBackend in Glow. We'd need to add options to specify the external compiler to use and may be the flags to pass to this compiler. It seems we don't need to support the JIT functionality for such cases as they are usually performing a cross-compilation.

title: Currently calling lower twice during profiling/quantization
author: jfix71
body: Right now we call lower() twice when doing profiling or quantization. E.g. for the Loader, we're calling lower() once prior to profiling or quantization inside Loader::compile(), and then again inside Backend::optimizeFunction(). We really only need to call lower() once. One simple solution here is to add a new option to CompilationOptions for skipLowering, set when we know we've already called lower() prior to calling compile(). Another more involved solution would be to move quantizeFunction()/profileQuantization() calls directly into Backend::optimizeFunction(), so that it could be done after lower(). This would require passing a lot of info through the ExecutionEngine::compile(), e.g. quantizationInfos, quantizationSchema, bindings, etc. (could be added to CompilationOptions).

title: Profile quantization consumes too much memory

body: The problem of scalability of quantization profile generation is addressed by: #2684 (minibatch) Nevertheless, at equal batch size, performing quantization profile generation increases a lot the memory requirement, compared to standard float inference. This is a problem I discussed with @opti-mix at the Glow workshop. For instance for a model we tested, it increases from 8GB to 50GB. The insertion of QuantizeProfile nodes prevent the merging of elementwise nodes and QuantizeProfile need extra tensors (histogram), but the memory increase should not be as huge. It turns out that the IR instruction scheduling (sinkAllocas ?) that targets reducing the live-range overlap of tensors doesn't work properly with QuantizationProfile nodes. When we dump the low-level Glow ir, we can see that QuantizedProfile nodes are all scheduled at the end. It has for effect to keep tensors of the model alive almost during the full model execution. I didn't investigate further yet. Is it a side effect of the in-out param of QuantizeProfile nodes, what may disturb the memory optimization (in-out param are alive permanently) ?

title: Add UInt8QTy ElemKind
author: jackm321
body: Create a UInt8QTy ElemKind and in mode loaders load uint8 quantized Tensors directly instead of converting to Int8QTy. Right now Glow has Int8QTy and when it loads Tensors from onnxifi that are uint_8 type, the loaded tensor is copied and shifted by -128 to make its values fit the expected range for Int8QTy. If Glow had a UInt8QTy ElemKind this copy and shifting could be avoided entirely. Furthermore, Glow has a UInt8FusedQTy which is supported by some operators and when an Int8QTy weight is loaded for this operator, it is then shifted back to fit the expected range of UInt8FusedQTy by adding 128 to all values in the Tensor which is an additional unnecessary overhead. Many of Glow's CPU and Interpreter op implementations support quantized tensors but only Int8QTy. These could be rewritten to support UInt8QTy but it may be easier to implement a graph transformation step (maybe using FunctionConverter) to convert Tensors of type UInt8QTy to Int8QTy during compilation on an as needed basis by the Backend.

title: Those macros that reference namespaced symbols should be defined outside any namespace
body: Those macros that reference namespaced symbols should be defined outside of any namespace, and explicit namespace resolution should be used for the symbols they reference. For example, take a look at the EXIT_ON_ERR macro defined in include/glow/Support/Error.h: /// Unwraps the T from within an llvm::Expected<T>. If the Expected<T> contains /// an error, the program will exit. #define EXIT_ON_ERR(...) (exitOnErr(__VA_ARGS__))  This macro references exitOnErr, which in turn is defined inside the glow namespace. That's not a problem per se as long as one globally exposes the entire glow namespace before using EXIT_ON_ERR. However, if we choose not to using namespace glow, then this is a problem. The following code won't compile (of course - this is not correct C++, as namespace resolution does not apply to preprocessor macros): glow::EXIT_ON_ERR(/* ... */)  Also, unless we expose the glow namespace with using namespace glow, the following code also won't compile: EXIT_ON_ERR(/* ... */)  In fact, the only way to get EXIT_ON_ERR to work is to expose all of the glow namespace with using namespace glow. Perhaps a better way to do this would be to pull such macros out of the glow namespace, and if they use anything from any namespace, then explicitly resolve the namespace. For instance: /// Unwraps the T from within an llvm::Expected<T>. If the Expected<T> contains /// an error, the program will exit. #define EXIT_ON_ERR(...) (glow::exitOnErr(__VA_ARGS__))

title: Proposal: constant folding on model load
author: Max-K-cadence
body: Hi, I have a proposal for a feature and I'd like to know if it can be accepted. The motivating example I have is following: Reshape(X, Gather(Shape(Y), const)) Currently, GLOW is unable to load models with such pattern. The reason is following: GLOW needs to statically know shapes of all output tensors. To know the output shape of Reshape, it needs its shape argument to be a constant. In my example, the model gets rejected because it is a Gather and not a constant. However, Shape(Y) is always a constant, and Gather(const, const) can actually be constant-folded. When it is done, we can load such model. More general statement of the problem: GLOW sometimes requires that some parameters are constants, but does not perform early constant-folding. Therefore, it rejects some models that it could load if it was done. The solution is following: we can introduce API to add method constantFold to a node. Iff all node inputs are constant, we can acquire their tensors and perform the same logic as in Interpreter backend. This will allow us to get static constant for such nodes instead of Instruction on load stage. The idea of code changes is following:  Introduce special flag to node builder that will add constant folding method on request; For each node for which we want to constant-fold, factor out its evaluation method from Interpreter backend to a separate function some ConstantFolding.h file; Now, both constant-fold method and Interpreter backend call this same function; In Model Loader, add logic like: if (Tensor *CF = node->tryConstantFold()) { <register constant for node>}.  I already have an implementation of this for Gather node that enables the said class of models. This can be expanded into a wider number of nodes incrementally. What do you guys think of that?

title: Question: MaxPoolWithArgmax - new node or new output to existing node?
author: Max-K-cadence
body: Hi, I'm working on #2974, and I have a design question to discuss before I come up with final version. In ONNX, MaxPool has an optional output that calculates ArgMax that we need to support. In GLOW, I did not find a mechanism to specify that an output is optional for some node. It means that if we have specified the output, we should at least initialize it correctly. There are two possible ways to implement this optional output. Approach 1 (which I currently have): I've introduced a new node MaxPoolWithArgmax and did not touch the existing node MaxPool. When we parse ONNX file, we create one or another node, depending on whether the 2nd output is specified. Then I hacked the computation methods in CPU and Interpreter backends so that the same functions can be used to handle both kinds of nodes. The upside of this approach is that it does not break any existing code. The downside is that we have some code duplication in sense of node declaration. Approach 2 (which we internally discuss): We could instead tweak MaxPool node to have 2 outputs, add a Boolean field signaling whether or not the 2nd output is actually calculated. It means that we should always initialize this 2nd output with some tensor, even if we never use it. The upside of that is less code duplication, and node's API will match those in ONNX. The downsides are:  We have this dummy type initialization whenever we create a node; Other (maybe downstream) backends may not compile if they create these nodes inside, so this may disrupt someone's work. If some backend is not aware that there can be this 2nd output, this may cause a more sneaky bug than just failure with unsupported node kind.  What do you guys think would be a better way to do it?

title: How to support TensorFlow operators that cannot be easily converted to ONNX?
author: Max-K-cadence
body: Hi, Sorry for long wall of text, I just want to give a comprehensive description of a problem I have and a solution I see. I have a conceptual question about how we can support nodes that are not described in ONNX format, but are described in TensorFlow format and there is no easy way to convert one to another. Specifically, I am working with a model that has ScatterNd node which is described here: https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/scatter_nd Conceptually, ScatterNd is pretty similar to Glow's ScatterAssign node, with two significant differences:  ScatterAssign only assigns (N-1)-dimensional slices to N-dimensional dest by 1-dimensional indices. ScatterNd may assign K-dimensional slices to N-dimensional dest by (N-K)-dimensional indices; ScatterNd allows duplication of indices. If some index is seen twice, their updates are summed.  Otherwise it does the same thing as ScatterAssign. Due to property 1), it is more generic. Along with property 2), ScatterNd is virtually a generalized version of "Scatter add" to a new destination. There are three possible ways how we can bring support of ScatterNd in glow: Approach 1: support it in tf2onnx converter There is an ongoing discussion about it here: onnx/tensorflow-onnx#455 Unfortunately, there is no simple mapping between ScatterNd and anything that ONNX currently supports. I've been studying it myself and came to same conclusion as @chinhuang007: implementing this conversion is going to be a lot of pain. I don't really believe it's going to happen soon. Approach 2: add this node to ONNX standard There is also a discussion about adding this node to ONNX standard: onnx/onnx#2074 (comment). There is some idea about mapping it to ONNX Scatter node, however the complexity of index conversion that needs to be done before it is very high. I don't see much progress on this way either. Approach 3: support ScatterNd as if it was an ONNX node, using TensorFlow specification We may just pretend that Approach 2 has worked, and ScatterNd is described in ONNX standard, and its description is a perfect match with that in TensorFlow. Then we can just support it in Glow. Given that Approaches 1 and 2 give no results for quite a time, I wanted to ask, can I follow Approach 3 in Glow project? Implementation here is not super-hard, I already have a working prototype for interpreter, however it is a conceptual question: can we create a precedent of introducing an "not yet described ONNX node"? Or we should only add nodes that are described in ONNX standard in Glow? If the answer to that is yes, then I'd like to describe how we can design the solution. After making a prototype (that uses a custom node lowered to custom instruction), I realized that it has a lot of common with existing ScatterAssign node. So the solution plan I suggest is the following:  We can change semantics of ScatterAssign so that it has property 1) (can set by multi-dimensional indices); We add a new node ScatterAdd that will be similar to ScatterAssign, with difference of supporting property 2) (accumulation for duplicating indices); Lower ScatterNd to this ScatterAdd node.  What do you think? Can we do this upstream? :)

title: [Bug] optimizeConversions is too optimistic about what casts are NOOP
author: Max-K-cadence
body: optimizeConversions unconditionally performs the following transform: T1 X = ...; T1 Y = T1(T2(X));  replace Y with X  It does not consider 2 important cases when this replacement is invalid:  T1 is a floating-point type, T2 is not. In this case, the conversion may drop fractional part and the entire thing is not a NOOP. T1 is a wider type than T2 (e.g. T1 is int64 and T2 is int32). In this case, cast may also lose significant senior bits.  In both this cases, the said replacement should be disabled. The bug was fund while I was adding more checks to test of #3179. Working on fix.

title: Loader must guard against unsupported backends in interpreter mode
body: When running model-runner (or in fact any model builder that uses the loader) in non-bundle-emitting mode, specifying -backend=CPU causes SIGSEGV. The loader (perhaps in Loader::runInference) must guard against this to make sure that the correct backend is created. title: Extend LLVMIRCodeGen to support compiling multiple Glow functions into a single LLVM Module or object file
author: opti-mix
body: A single glow::Module may contain multiple glow::Functions. It could happen e.g. when Glow uses partitioning or if we would introduce scheduling of subgraphs for parallel execution, etc. It may be very useful to compile these multiple functions together into the same LLVM module or into the same object file. To achieve this, some changes in the LLVMIRCodeGen may be required. Here are some possible LLVMIRCodeGen changes:  When compiling an IRFunction, allow the LLVMBackend to re-use an already existing LLVM module if it is present. This would allow to add more functions to the same module. Or continue compiling each IRFunction into its own module, but use LLVM's Linker APIs to link those modules together before starting any LLVM optimizations. BTW, the libjit bitcode is currently read/included into each LLVM module created for each IRFunction. This could be changed to create a separate LLVM module for the libjit and then link the LLVM module(s) produced from an IRFunction (or multiple IRFunctions) with it. And of course, one should take care of function names to avoid possible name conflicts. Each IRFunction should produce an LLVM::Function with a unique name. All other generated helper LLVM functions should be marked as local to the module, unless they are supposed to be shared by multiple modules (e.g. libjit functions are likely to have a linkage which allows to use them from other modules).
