title: Support Backend Specific Node Verifiers
author: nickgg
body: Currently Node Verification is Backend independent, but there are components of the Node that depend on the backend for validity. Some examples:  Different backends have different dimensional limits for various Nodes (e.g. CPU/Interp is limited to 6 dimensions for BatchedReduceAdd, but OCL is limited to 4). Tensor Alignment will be phased in to some backends before others. Fused Activations are supported on specific backends only (initially just Habana). OpenCL has a limitation on the group parameter for Convolutions which doesn't exist on other backends.  The way we handle this currently is to put asserts in the backend specific code when executing these instructions, but this is brittle and spread through various places in the code. We should be able to tell if a Function is valid at compile time. To fix this, we could add a Verify() method to Backend which can be overriden to handle these backend specific checks - similar to how transformPostLowering works now.

title: Teach Glow how to support layout requirements for nodes and tensors
author: shajrawi
body: Taking the tensor layouts portion out of #2686 as alignment requirements have already been done and this is a different issue. Quoting @opti-mix :  Different operations (e.g. convolutions, gemms, etc) may require each of their inputs and outputs to use a specific memory layout, both in terms of alignments and logical ordering of dimensions (e.g. NHWC or NCHW). More over, these requirements may depend on the properties of the operation, e.g. dimensions of its operands, etc. E.g. a convolution with a small filter may need the input operands in a format different from a convolution with a big filter. Today, Glow core and custom backends implicitly hard-code this knowledge about the operations into (backend-specific) nodes and code that works with them, i.e. in the code that transforms Glow nodes, which are in the canonical NHWC format, into backend-specific nodes. This is pretty fragile and involves a lot of boiler plate code. What if Glow would be able to ask a backend for each node what are the requirements for each of node's inputs and results in terms of alignments and ordering of dimensions?   The backend would return this information and Glow core could insert all the required layout transformations using a new node called LayoutTransform (may be we could extend/subsume Transpose for these purposes).   This new LayoutTransform node could be applied to Constant weights at compile-time. It can also be optimized in almost the same ways as Glow optimizes Transpose nodes, e.g. multiple LayoutTransforms can be combined into one, opposite LayoutTransforms can eliminate each other, etc.   This way all of the functionality to insert the required layout transforms is handled by the Glow core, which removes a lot of code duplication from backends. It also allows for better optimizations as the optimizer would understand the semantics of LayoutTransform. And it also allows for better verification, as Glow can now check that layouts of all inputs/outputs of each node satisfy the requirements of this operation as reported by backends.    To expand on this idea I'd like to share an idea by @artemrakhov  first start with a "raw" state of uncompliance, where we insert LayoutTransformation nodes while needed. Then we have a loop to sink and clamp layout transformations together, similarly to what we do to transposes. In fact, LayoutTransformation is generalization of Transpose, since we can not only change the order of dimensions, but also their alignments.  Basically, we need to port/expand transpose syncing / elimination optimization to support layouts. Additionally, I think that if we pursue this direction, It should also include a verifier that makes sure that a node A that expects certain layout constraints for its input have said constraints satisfied after doing layout transformations. This would clean-up node creation in Graph.cpp and create a central location for satisfying layout-constraints. Consider static void assertConv3DDims for example, as the name suggests it does some checks to make sure the tensor layout and dimensions make sense. such tests could be moved into a central location: the proposed layout verifier. Another useful outcome of this work is simplifying model-import: We (currently) silently add a transpose before some nodes because we may have them in a non-Glow-compliant layout. Take Bucketize from Caffee2 for example: The Caffe2 operator supports NCHW layout while we, in Glow, do not. When importing from Caffe2 we check for NCHW layout and add a transpose. We can make the import process for a large number of operators way more intuitive if we don't hard-code a transpose node but add them via layout requirements. If we support such a change for model loaders, A tricky situation that we'd need to tackle is knowing the original layout that we imported. We have that knowledge when we import from say Caffe2, but, we don't keep track of it in Glow. One possible solution to this problem is if we included that information in Placeholders (and constants?).

title: LIBJIT memory allocation should be switchable between static/dynamic

body: Problem File: "libjit_matmul.cpp" Function: "libjit_matmul_outer" In the old days, the buffer "packedB" was statically allocated:  float packedB[kc * nc] attribute((aligned(64)));  Recently it has been changed to use dynamic memory allocation:  float *packedB = nullptr; if (pack) { libjit_aligned_malloc((void **)&packedB, 64, kc * nc); }  When cross-compiling bundles for bare-metal targets (no OS, no dynamic memory allocation), the bundle ends up with having the undefined symbol "posix_memalign". author: shajrawi
body: We're creating an Interpreter backend, but we are also running constant folding after lowering. This can be bad on backends that create transformations that break Glow's canonical tensor layout. See NonSquarePaddingConvolution on the OpenCL backend for example. We have a Reshape node in NCHW layout. Constant folding creates the following function for it: Graph structure __constEvaluationFunction__: Reshape name : conv_filter1 Input : float<2 x 2 x 2 x 1> Dims : [2, 1, 2, 2] Layout : NCHW users : 1 Result : float<2 x 1 x 2 x 2> Save name : conv_filter11 Input : float<2 x 1 x 2 x 2> Output : float<2 x 1 x 2 x 2> users : 0  If we run a canonical layout verifier on said function, see #3452, it is gonna blow up: Save is getting NCHW layout but expects NHWC layout. The constant function that we created is bad.

title: RecommendationSystemTest should use HostManager instead of ExecutionEngine
author: opti-mix
body: RecommendationSystemTest currently uses ExecutionEngine, which is OK. But due to this fact the functionality of this test are a bit limited for the following scenarios:   It is impossible to test with concurrent requests, because ExecutionEngine does not support concurrent execution   It is impossible to test with heterogeneous partitioning, because ExecutionEngine supports only a single backend at a time. But heterogeneous partitioning use-cases are very important for bringing up new backends, which support only a subset of operations required by the full RecommendationSystemTest model.   Therefore, it would be better to use HostManager instead of ExecutionEngine to overcome the limitations mentioned above.

title: [Interpreter] Unexpected results when using ffast-math
author: et-nivard
body: Current Release mode build uses ffast-math. This is producing unexpected results in some cases with respect to Debug mode compilation. There is a related PR going on but won't be fixing this issue  #2960 One clear example that shows this kind of issues is the AdaptiveAvgPoolInst implementation. It contains this define: #define END_IND(a, b, c) (size_t) std::ceil((float)(((a) + 1) * (c)) / (b)) When a = 2, c = 7, and b = 7, it outputs 4 instead of 3 provided last iteration loop runs on c. ffast-math will approximate (a+1)/b increment and cause small error that gets maximized by ceil function. Provided that Interpreter is usually regarded as a reference we could skip ffast-math flag at least when compiling this backend.

title: Tensor::isEqual() not aware of padding
author: et-nivard
body: Current implementation of Tensor::isEqual() does not support tensors with padding. It just performs a plain traverse https://github.com/pytorch/glow/blob/master/include/glow/Base/Tensor.h#L817 without skipping padding positions. Also, it uses size() instead of actualSize() so it misses last elements when padding exists. An update is required to iterate over all valid elements while skipping pad-elements.

I'm getting the following compilation problem: glow/lib/LLVMIRCodeGen/BundleSaver.cpp: In member function â€˜void glow::BundleSaver::saveHeader(llvm::StringRef)â€™: glow/include/glow/Base/DimType.h:41:17: error: expected â€˜)â€™ before â€˜PRIu64â€™  #define PRIuDIM PRIu64                  ^ glow/lib/LLVMIRCodeGen/BundleSaver.cpp:293:35: note: in expansion of macro â€˜PRIuDIMâ€™          shapeStr += strFormat("%" PRIuDIM ", ", dims[idx]);  The reason of this is that at the point where <cinttypes> was first included to this file, __STDC_FORMAT_MACROS was not defined. title: Chain of arithmetic ops with Constants should fold into BatchNorm
author: vuzelac-cadence
body: We have a few disjoint optimizations that we would like to consolidate and upstream. We are looking to fold a chain of arithmetic operations w/ Constant into a BatchNorm (BN), whenever the chain is preceded by Convolution or BN:  If Convolution, fold the chain into BN (This BN is folded into Conv in other optimization). Merge with BatchNorm above the chain (could just create a BN like above, and have a separate step to merge consecutive BNs).  The issue I have is about examining the Constants in RHS/LHS of the arithmetic operations; broadcasts/tiles/constants are already folded into a bigger constant into the importer. So, to examine if the constant is a broadcasted one, we would need to compare it's tensors across the channel dimension. This computation is relatively demanding and all it does is to annulate the constant folding, as all we do is to extract the original constant. We already have this optimization in a few places and now looking to improve it. However, I just don't see the way out of this excessive computation; we can't import many models/operators w/o the constant folding being enabled in the importer. Do you have any other ideas ?

title: [Bundle][Feature] Error handling in LIBJIT with a return error code.
author: mciprian13
body: This is more like a nice to have feature of having LIBJIT functions to do some error handling and dropping a value of 0 (no error) vs something else to report problems. For example the main bundle entry function could have the following prototype: uint32_t resnet50(uint8_t *constantWeight, uint8_t *mutableWeight, uint8_t *activations); that is to return an error code if something happens. For the main LIBJIT math functions this is not necessarily very useful but for custom LIBJIT functions (e.g. DMA transfers, Remote Procedure Calls, etc) this is extremely useful. The main bundle function could have a local variable uint32_t errorCode initialized with 0 and maybe have an option in LLVMIRgen for createCall called errorCheck which does bitwise OR between errorCode and the uint32_t returned by the function (or this could be done unconditionally by createCall for all the libjit functions which return an uint32_t). Lastly the bundle would return errorCode.

title: Provide pass pipeline mechanisms for low-level IR passes
author: opti-mix
body: Glow provides pass pipeline mechanisms for graph-level optimizations and transformations. We've got some requests to provide similar mechanisms for low-level IR passes. Ideally, it would be nice to have a general pass pipeline mechanism that can work with any kind of IR, e.g. with backend-specific IRs as well. It seems like an easy way to achieve it would be to copy & adjust the existing graph-level pass pipeline machinery for low-level IR pass pipelines. But it may introduce a lot of code duplication. Alternatively, one could try to generalize the existing  pass pipeline machinery  to support any kind of passes and IRs (e.g. by parameterizing pipeline-related classes using template parameters representing the IR related types, etc). This would be more future-proof, but may eventually complicate the code and also introduce some linking issues or unwanted dependencies.

title: [ConstantFolding] Need to preserve Placeholders count and name for Module
author: jfix71
body: Constant folding in the loader is currently creating Placeholders without erasing them from the Module when finished with them. These Placeholders are orphaned and never used again. They are created here:                glow/include/glow/Importer/ProtobufLoader.h                   Lines 316 to 317       in       0accffe                                                 Placeholder *PH =                                               F->getParent()->createPlaceholder(r.getType(), outputName, false);                     Additionally, the above line is using names of Placeholders that we may want for actual Placeholders. Even if these Placeholders are later on erased (which they currently aren't as mentioned above) their names are taken up as already used/unique and so future Placeholders would not be able to use the same name. In more detail, in the above code snippet we are simply using the outputName for the Save which creates a Placeholder with name outputName to save into. For example, if the op we're constant folding is directly used as an output with name out1, then we will create a Placeholder by name out1 here during ConstantFolding. Then later on when we call ONNXModelLoader::setOutputNodes(), we'd try to create a new Placeholder named out1 but it'd be uniqued to name out1__1. BTW, we probably should also verify that inputs and outputs do in fact get the name they ask for when we create them in the ONNXModelLoader. CC: @ksaurabh-cadence

title: [Node][Verification] Incorrect Conv/Pool node verification !!!!!
author: mciprian13
body: The current way one of the H/W dimensions is validated in Glow for Conv/Pool node is like this: expectedOutputH = (inputH + padTop + padBottom - effKernelH) / strideH + 1  where effKernelH is the effective dilated kernel size: effKernelH = dilationH * (kernelH - 1) + 1  but for strides higher than 1 this is incorrect due to the integer division (which floors the result) resulting in possible inconsistent Conv/Pool nodes in the graph. The correct way is to compare the expected input size like this: expectedInputH = (outputH - 1) * strideH - padTop - padBottom + effKernelH  I ran over this when working on the node splitting infrastructure #4438 which identified places in the Glow unit tests where such ill-defined nodes are used.

title: [AvgPool] Add flag to not include pads when normalizing
author: mciprian13
body: The current implementation of AvgPool always normalizes by the window size regardless of whether the window includes padding or not. Even the ONNX format specifies a boolean flag count_include_pad which defaults to 0 which means that the normalization is done by the number of samples within the window excluding pads (this means the current implementation of AvgPool does not comply to the ONNX definition). For generality we should have a flag countPads which should allow both flavors of the implementation.

title: Automatic RNN state tracking is not working / Recurrent projection weights are optimized out
author: oleksii-abramenko
body: Hello community, Please consider toy neural net defined in the following way: class RNNTest(nn.Module):     def __init__(self):         super(RNNTest, self).__init__()         self.rnn = nn.RNN(60, 60, num_layers=3)      def forward(self, x):         x, _ = self.rnn(x)         return x  Total number of params for this model is 21960 It is exported to ONNX using the following method:  model = RNNTest() dummy_input = torch.randn(1,1,60) model = model.eval() torch.onnx.export(model, (dummy_input,), "test.onnx",                   input_names=['data'] ,training=torch.onnx.TrainingMode.EVAL)   It is compiled with GLOW by the following command: ./model-compiler -model test.onnx -emit-bundle test_dir  -model-input=data,float,[1,1,60] -backend=CPU -target=arm -mcpu=cortex-m4 -float-abi=hard After exporting, it is evident that file test.weights.bin has size 44,736, which is not expected because it should be at least 21960*4bytes = 87840 bytes, given the fact that all parameters are floats. Upon further inspection it seems like recurrent the projection weights have been optimized out. I think this may happen because compiler sees that initial state of RNN is not provided(which means it is zero) and doesn't have effect on further computation. At the same time I see that GLOW automatically creates and exposes placeholders for hidden states to enable easy state manipulation and automatic tracking. But this is not helpful at this time because RNN is not working properly due to the weights being optimized out. In order to prevent recurrent projection weights from being optimized out one need to modify the model to provide hidden state explicitly as a placeholder: class RNNTest(nn.Module):     def __init__(self):         super(RNNTest, self).__init__()         self.rnn = nn.RNN(60, 60, num_layers=3)      def forward(self, x, h):         x, _ = self.rnn(x, h)         return x  dummy_input = torch.randn(1,1,60) dummy_hidden = torch.randn(3, 1, 60) inf_model = inf_model.eval() torch.onnx.export(inf_model, (dummy_input, dummy_hidden), "test.onnx",                   input_names=['data', 'hidden'] ,training=torch.onnx.TrainingMode.EVAL)  ./model-compiler -model test.onnx -emit-bundle test_dir  -model-input=data,float,[1,1,60] -model-input=hidden,float,[3,1,60] -backend=CPU -target=arm -mcpu=cortex-m4 -float-abi=hard  In this case upon the conversion our test.weights.bin will have size of 87,936 bytes, so that the recurrent projection matrix is not optimized out. So the question is: Why do you automatically create and expose placeholders for hidden states, if it is anyway required to provide your own placeholder for hidden state in order to prevent graph optimization? And in this case one cannot track states automatically, it is required to do manual memcpy() to copy hidden states from your automatic placeholders to the input placeholder "hidden" Is there any way how to prevent compiler from optimizing out the recurrent projection when the hidden state is not explicitly provided as input? This will allow to take advantages of your "automatic hidden state tracking" mechanism. Thanks in advance!

This leads to suboptimal optimization, e..g, loop vectorization inserts explicit memory region overlap checks in the final binary code. I suggest making this change diff --git a/lib/LLVMIRCodeGen/Pipeline.cpp b/lib/LLVMIRCodeGen/Pipeline.cpp index d9aa3ac4..47b340a8 100644 --- a/lib/LLVMIRCodeGen/Pipeline.cpp +++ b/lib/LLVMIRCodeGen/Pipeline.cpp @@ -69,9 +69,6 @@ LLVMIRGen::getInlinineAttr(const llvm::Function *F) const {  }    void LLVMIRGen::updateInlineAttributes(llvm::Module *M) { -  // An empty attribute set to replace the target-specific machine code -  // attributes that were attached by the frontend. -  llvm::AttributeList AL;    for (auto &FF : *M) {      if (FF.isDeclaration()) {        continue; @@ -87,8 +84,12 @@ void LLVMIRGen::updateInlineAttributes(llvm::Module *M) {            << "Unknown inlining attribute returned by getInlinineAttr";        dontInline = (inlineAttr == llvm::Attribute::AttrKind::NoInline);      } -    // Clear all attributes. -    FF.setAttributes(AL); +    // Replace the target-specific machine code function attributes that were  +    // attached by the frontend. Keep return and parameter attributes, e.g., +    // noalias. +    FF.setAttributes( +      FF.getAttributes().removeAttributes(M->getContext(), +                                          llvm::AttributeList::FunctionIndex));      // Force inline all non-no-inline functions.      if (!dontInline || alwaysInline) {        FF.addFnAttr(llvm::Attribute::AttrKind::AlwaysInline);   to only clear the function attributes and leave the return and parameter attributes alone. A better fix would be to only remove the unwanted target-specific machine code function attributes, but that would require more work, esp. to identify what is wanted (inline/noinline) what is not .

title: [Quantization] Make quantization parameters part of the constant weights
author: mciprian13
body: @opti-mix @jfix71 We have an internal usecase in which we want the following:  Pre-compile a given quantized model (say TensorFlowLite) to a bundle and link it as part of the target run-time (the target is an MCU) We have some high-level front-end tools capable to retrain the same model with different data What we want is to update the model at run-time without re-compiling the run-time application:  In principle this would consist only in changing the model weights (since the model is the same and so should be the bundle) but for quantized models the quantized parameters are embedded in the bundle program and since a retraining changes the quantization parameters then we need also to update them as well   Therefore what we need is to make the quantization parameters part of the weights buffer so they are dynamically read at run-time. This provides the flexibility we need. Some side effects would be that we lose the constant propagation for them.  So I have two questions:  Technically how hard does this seem to do and what (if any) technical problems do you see? How open are you to have this modification in the upstream?

title: [GraphOptimizer] Reshape sinking
author: aturetsk
body: While Reshape nodes are noops and do not directly contribute to model execution time, having them in a graph might prevent other optimizations/transformations from happening. So, sinking Reshapes (similar to Transposes) and merging them might potentially lead to better optimized graph. One particular use case I encountered is coming from OptimizeTransposeIntoReshape optimization (#2630). There was a Transpose in a graph which Glow wasn't able to optimize out in a single glow::optimize run, so it sank till a specific point and then became a Reshape. On the next glow::optimize iteration, while conditions for further Transpose sinking were satisfied, it didn't happen because it was a Reshape now, not Transpose. Having Reshape sinking logic along with Transpose sinking should help to resolve such cases. So, does it make sense to have Reshape sinking transformations in GraphOptimizer? Also, I've noticed there is a transformation in Glow which is opposite to Reshape sinking - Reshape hoisting over Clip (#4074). @jfix71, could you give any comment on why we would do that?

title: Add support for auto_pad=NOTSET in ONNXModelLoader
author: mciprian13
body: When I compile the following model mini_xception.zip with the command: model-compiler -backend=CPU -model=mini_xception.onnx -emit-bundle=bundle -onnx-define-symbol=N,1  the importer crashes with the following message: Error message: only auto_pad==VALID, SAME_UPPER and SAME_LOWER are supported  The error comes from the following place:                glow/lib/Importer/ONNXModelLoader.cpp                   Lines 1189 to 1190       in       46166b2                                                 return MAKE_ERR(                                               "only auto_pad==VALID, SAME_UPPER and SAME_LOWER are supported");                     Based on my understanding of the ONNX standard:  If the auto_pad=NOTSET then the explicit attribute pads is used (which if does not exist then if default to 0 for start/end of each spatial axis)

title: [torch_glow] undefined symbol when importing torch_glow
author: balaram-cadence
body: I built pytorch from source and also followed directions in https://github.com/pytorch/glow/blob/master/docs/pytorch.md to make sure torch_glow can be built. When I run tests however, I get undefined symbol error when importing torch_glow. title: Conv - Relu - BatchNorm WRONG FUSION
author: LuisTbx
body: On the BatchNorm paper the order of the layers is: Conv + BN + ReLU. And when this order is respected, the fusion of Conv and BN can be performed without any problem. But, when the order is Conv + ReLU + BN the fusion should not be performed as it leads to numerically different results. As part of the optimizations done in GLOW the Conv gets always fused to the BN, regardless of the ReLU in between, creating errors on the graph output. This issue need to be addressed, on the meantime I'm wondering: can we pass a compilation flag to do not perform this fusion?  I know there are flags, i just could not find the specific one to disable the Conv+BN one.
